Parameter sharing and anchor points (shared subwords across languages) are crucial for the emergence of cross-lingual representations in multilingual encoders.
Not all languages are equally represented in mBERT; low-resource languages suffer from poor performance due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
Explicit alignment methods, such as contrastive alignment using bitext, can improve cross-lingual representations, but their effectiveness varies across models and language pairs.
Zero-shot cross-lingual transfer exhibits high variance due to underspecified optimization, and data projection with self-training can constrain and improve transfer performance.
papers.limitation: mBERT performs poorly on low-resource languages due to limited pretraining data and vocabulary coverage.
future_direction: Continue scaling multilingual encoders to more languages and larger models
Extend to multimodal multilingual models
Improve cross-lingual transfer for low-resource languages
papers.abstract: NLP systems typically require support for more than one language. As different languages have different amounts of supervision, cross-lingual transfer benefits languages with little to no training data by transferring from other languages. From an engineering perspective, multilingual NLP benefits development and maintenance by serving multiple languages with a single system. Both cross-lingual transfer and multilingual NLP rely on cross-lingual representations serving as the foundation. As BERT revolutionized representation learning and NLP, it also revolutionized cross-lingual representations and cross-lingual transfer. Multilingual BERT was released as a replacement for single-language BERT, trained with Wikipedia data in 104 languages. Surprisingly, without any explicit cross-lingual signal, multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual representations in addition to representations for individual languages. This thesis first shows such surprising cross-lingual effectiveness compared against prior art on various tasks. Naturally, it raises a set of questions, most notably how do these multilingual encoders learn cross-lingual representations. In exploring these questions, this thesis will analyze the behavior of multilingual models in a variety of settings on high and low resource languages. We also look at how to inject different cross-lingual signals into multilingual encoders, and the optimization behavior of cross-lingual transfer with these models. Together, they provide a better understanding of multilingual encoders on cross-lingual transfer. Our findings will lead us to suggested improvements to multilingual encoders and cross-lingual transfer.

papers.title: What Is One Grain of Sand in the Desert? Analyzing Individual Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: How can we identify and analyze individual neurons in deep NLP models? The paper also investigates how localized or distributed linguistic properties are, whether neurons are exclusive to certain properties, and how information distribution differs between NMT and NLM.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes two methods for identifying and analyzing individual neurons in deep NLP models: a supervised Linguistic Correlation Analysis and an unsupervised Cross-model Correlation Analysis, and demonstrates their effectiveness through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes two methods for extracting salient neurons and demonstrates their accuracy through ablation experiments, with potential applications in model distillation and neural architecture search.
papers.key_findings:
Open class categories (e.g., verb, location) are more distributed across neurons than closed class categories (e.g., coordinating conjunction, determiner).
The model recognizes a hierarchy of linguistic properties and distributes neurons accordingly.
Important neurons extracted from Cross-model Correlation overlap with those from Linguistic Correlation (e.g., position neurons).
Ablating top neurons identified by Cross-model Correlation causes significant performance drop, validating the method.
Using only top neurons, classifiers can regain much of the performance, suggesting potential for model distillation.
future_direction: Applying the methods to model distillation and neural architecture search
Exploring recent architectures like Transformer and QRNN
papers.abstract: Despite the remarkable evolution of deep neural networks in natural language processing (NLP), their interpretability remains a challenge. Previous work largely focused on what these models learn at the representation level. We break this analysis down further and study individual dimensions (neurons) in the vector representation learned by end-to-end neural models in NLP tasks. We propose two methods: Linguistic Correlation Analysis, based on a supervised method to extract the most relevant neurons with respect to an extrinsic task, and Cross-model Correlation Analysis, an unsupervised method to extract salient neurons w.r.t. the model itself. We evaluate the effectiveness of our techniques by ablating the identified neurons and reevaluating the network’s performance for two tasks: neural machine translation (NMT) and neural language modeling (NLM). We further present a comprehensive analysis of neurons with the aim to address the following questions: i) how localized or distributed are different linguistic properties in the models? ii) are certain neurons exclusive to some properties and not others? iii) is the information more or less distributed in NMT vs. NLM? and iv) how important are the neurons identified through the linguistic correlation method to the overall task? Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit (Dalvi et al. 2019a). This paper is a non-archived version of the paper published at AAAI (Dalvi et al. 2019b).

papers.title: Language Models Linearly Represent Sentiment
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is sentiment represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in the residual stream of LLMs across multiple models and tasks, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is summarized at intermediate tokens like commas and names.
papers.conclusion: The study concludes that sentiment is linearly represented in LLMs and identifies a summarization motif as a key mechanism for sentiment processing, providing a detailed case study for analyzing feature representation in activation space.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly as a single direction in the residual stream across a range of transformer-based language models.
The sentiment direction found on simple toy datasets generalizes to real-world sentiment analysis tasks like SST and IMDB.
The sentiment direction is causally important for sentiment tasks; intervening on it can flip model predictions.
A 'summarization motif' exists: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens (e.g., commas, periods, names) without inherent valence, and this summarized information is causally relevant.
Ablating the sentiment direction at comma positions alone significantly reduces classification accuracy, demonstrating the functional importance of the summarization motif.
future_direction: Deeper investigation of the summarization motif circuitry
Exploring neurons that write to the sentiment direction further

papers.title: Interpreting Recurrent and Attention-Based Neural Models: a Case Study on Natural Language Inference
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the intermediate layers of neural models for natural language inference by visualizing the saliency of attention and LSTM gating signals?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces saliency-based visualization strategies for interpreting attention and LSTM gating signals in neural models for natural language inference, revealing insights not available from traditional methods.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization strategies effectively interpret neural models for NLI, offering new insights into model behavior and potential for improving models in future work.
papers.key_findings:
Attention saliency maps highlight which word alignments are critical for model decisions, unlike standard attention visualizations which may appear similar across different predictions.
Comparing models via attention saliency shows that ESIM-300 focuses on gender connections (e.g., 'John' vs 'man') while ESIM-50 does not, explaining performance differences.
LSTM gating signal saliency norms show that inference LSTM layers concentrate on key parts of sentences, whereas input LSTM layers have more spread-out saliency.
Saliency patterns for LSTM gates are consistent across different gates within the same layer, allowing joint interpretation.
The proposed visualization methods provide complementary understanding by revealing how models process information differently for contradiction, neutral, and entailment cases.
future_direction: Extend the study to other NLP tasks and models.
papers.abstract: Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in natural language inference (NLI) tasks. While these models are widely explored, they are hard to interpret and it is often unclear how and why they actually work. In this paper, we take a step toward explaining such deep learning based models through a case study on a popular neural model for NLI. In particular, we propose to interpret the intermediate layers of NLI models by visualizing the saliency of attention and LSTM gating signals. We present several examples for which our methods are able to reveal interesting insights and identify the critical information contributing to the model decisions.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Correcting Negative Bias in Large Language Models through Negative Attention Score Alignment
papers.research_question: What causes negative bias in large language models during binary decision tasks requiring complex reasoning, and how can it be corrected through attention head analysis and tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Negative Attention Score (NAS) to quantify negative bias in LLMs and proposes NASA, a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that corrects bias by aligning attention heads identified via NAS.
papers.conclusion: NASA effectively mitigates negative bias in LLMs for binary decision tasks and serves as a useful interpretability framework for analyzing attention heads.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit negative bias in binary decision tasks, showing high precision but low recall and higher confidence for negative responses.
NAS correlates with negative confidence and identifies query-agnostic negative attention heads across domains.
NASA reduces the precision-recall gap and improves F1 scores while preserving general reasoning abilities.
NASA enhances model calibration by aligning prediction confidence with accuracy.
Fine-tuning negative attention heads in order based on NAS is effective, whereas random tuning leads to suboptimal results.
papers.limitation:
Further research is needed to understand the causes and mechanisms behind negative biases in LLMs.
Fine-tuning attention heads individually may not be time-efficient; more efficient training methods could be explored.
future_direction: Explore more time-efficient training methods for tuning attention heads.
Investigate integrated research approaches connecting various elements of negative bias.
papers.abstract: A binary decision task, like yes-no questions or answer verification, reflects a significant real-world scenario such as where users look for confirmation about the correctness of their decisions on specific issues. In this work, we observe that language models exhibit a negative bias in the binary decisions of complex reasoning tasks. Based on our observations and the rationale about attention-based model dynamics, we propose a negative attention score (NAS) to systematically and quantitatively formulate negative bias. Based on NAS, we identify attention heads that attend to negative tokens provided in the instructions as answer candidate of binary decisions, regardless of the question in the prompt, and validate their association with the negative bias. Additionally, we propose the negative attention score alignment (NASA) method, which is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique to address the extracted negatively biased attention heads. Experimental results from various domains of reasoning tasks and large model search space demonstrate that NASA significantly reduces the gap between precision and recall caused by negative bias while preserving their generalization abilities.

papers.title: Language-Specific Neurons Do Not Facilitate Cross-Lingual Transfer
papers.research_question: This work explores whether existing techniques to identify language-specific neurons can be leveraged to enhance cross-lingual task performance of low-resource languages.
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that test-time interventions and fine-tuning of language-specific neurons in multilingual LLMs are insufficient to yield meaningful improvements in cross-lingual task performance for low-resource languages.
papers.conclusion: Language-specific neurons do not function independently but interact with broader model components, and need further investigation as tools of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.key_findings:
Test-time interventions on language-specific neurons do not improve cross-lingual task performance and often disrupt task-relevant information.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons using LoRA does not lead to significant improvements in downstream task performance.
Setting neuron activations to zero does not significantly degrade task performance, suggesting zero is not a true indicator of deactivation.
Language-specific neurons are polysemantic and not independent, which limits the effectiveness of targeted interventions.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on language-specific neurons in the MLP layers, excluding attention mechanisms which may also play a significant role.
Experiments use a limited number of languages and datasets, limiting generalizability.
Interventions rely on statistical activations computed from Wikipedia text, which might not fully capture task-specific behavior.
Does not explore alternate methods of fine-tuning techniques that might yield better results.

papers.title: A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.
papers.key_findings:
Zero-layer transformers model bigram statistics, accessible directly from weights.
One-layer attention-only transformers are ensembles of bigram and skip-trigram models, enabling simple in-context learning.
Two-layer attention-only transformers implement induction heads through attention head composition, allowing more complex in-context learning.
Induction heads use a sophisticated algorithm to repeat previous sequences based on token similarity.
The framework allows direct analysis of weight matrices to understand model behavior without running the model.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on attention-only transformers, excluding MLP layers which are harder to interpret.
Preliminary and not applied to larger, more complex models.
future_direction: Apply the framework to larger and more realistic models.
Investigate MLP layers in transformers.
papers.abstract: How can we reverse engineer the internal computations of transformer language models using a mathematical framework? Introduces a mathematical framework for understanding transformer circuits, enabling reverse engineering of small attention-only models and identifying induction heads as key for in-context learning. The mathematical framework provides a foundation for understanding transformer circuits, with induction heads as a critical component for in-context learning, paving the way for future work on larger models.

papers.title: Copy Suppression: Comprehensively Understanding an Attention Head
papers.research_question: What is the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small across the entire training distribution?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and explains the copy suppression mechanism of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small, showing it suppresses naive copying to improve calibration and accounts for 76.9% of the head's impact.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces copy suppression as the main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small and verifies it mechanistically using weights-based analysis of QK and OV circuits, providing a comprehensive explanation of a component in a language model.
papers.key_findings:
The main role of attention head L10H7 in GPT-2 Small is copy suppression, which explains 76.9% of its behavior on the training distribution.
Copy suppression reduces model loss and improves calibration by suppressing incorrect token predictions that appear earlier in context.
Copy suppression is a mechanism for self-repair, explaining 39% of self-repair in the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task.
The OV circuit of L10H7 suppresses the tokens it attends to, with 84.70% of tokens having their diagonal as one of the top 10 most negative values.
The QK circuit of L10H7 attends to tokens that are predicted at the query position, with 95.72% of diagonal values being the largest in their rows.
papers.limitation:
The idealised setup for analyzing the QK circuit does not completely faithfully represent L10H7's real functioning.
Using KL divergence as an ablation metric has limitations, as discussed in Appendix J.
papers.abstract: We present a single attention head in GPT-2 Small that has one main role across the entire training distribution. If components in earlier layers predict a certain token, and this token appears earlier in the context, the head suppresses it: we call this copy suppression. Attention Head 10.7 (L10H7) suppresses naive copying behavior which improves overall model calibration. This explains why multiple prior works studying certain narrow tasks found negative heads that systematically favored the wrong answer. We uncover the mechanism that the Negative Heads use for copy suppression with weights-based evidence and are able to explain 76.9% of the impact of L10H7 in GPT-2 Small. To the best of our knowledge, this is the most comprehensive description of the complete role of a component in a language model to date. One major effect of copy suppression is its role in self-repair. Self-repair refers to how ablating crucial model components results in downstream neural network parts compensating for this ablation. Copy suppression leads to self-repair: if an initial overconfident copier is ablated, then there is nothing to suppress. We show that self-repair is implemented by several mechanisms, one of which is copy suppression, which explains 39% of the behavior in a narrow task. Interactive visualisations of the copy suppression phenomena may be seen at our web app https://copy-suppression.streamlit.app/

papers.title: Calibrating Factual Knowledge in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in Pretrained Language Models without re-training from scratch?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes CALINET, a lightweight method to calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs by adding and training new parameters (calibration memory slots) while freezing the original model, effectively reducing false knowledge and generalizing to downstream tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper reassesses knowledge in PLMs with CKA, proposes CALINET to calibrate knowledge at scale without updating original parameters, and shows it generalizes well to downstream tasks, with neuron-level investigations into the calibration mechanism.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Knowledge Assessment (CKA) reveals that nearly 50% of facts are stored incorrectly in PLMs.
CALINET effectively calibrates false facts, reducing the False Rate from 48.10% to 17.09% for T5-base on 100 facts.
CALINET generalizes calibrated knowledge to downstream question answering tasks, improving performance on calibration subsets without harming performance on other questions.
Analysis shows that calibration memory slots are more knowledge-intensive than original FFN values, with nearly 80% corresponding to meaningful concepts.
CALINET adjusts the output token distribution to increase the probability of the correct fact and its synonyms, indicating generalized calibration.
papers.limitation:
Relies on existing knowledge bases and synthetic data for assessment and calibration, which may not fully capture real-world knowledge complexity.
Evaluates PLMs via their predictions, which is a biased approach and may not accurately assess factual knowledge correctness.
Cannot completely calibrate all factual errors in PLMs.
future_direction: Improve calibration applicability in reality by moving beyond synthetic data.
Develop more accurate methods for assessing factual knowledge correctness in PLMs.
Develop more advanced knowledge calibration methods.
papers.abstract: Previous literature has proved that Pretrained Language Models (PLMs) can store factual knowledge. However, we find that facts stored in the PLMs are not always correct. It motivates us to explore a fundamental question: How do we calibrate factual knowledge in PLMs without re-training from scratch? In this work, we propose a simple and lightweight method CaliNet to achieve this goal. To be specific, we first detect whether PLMs can learn the right facts via a contrastive score between right and fake facts. If not, we then use a lightweight method to add and adapt new parameters to specific factual texts. Experiments on the knowledge probing task show the calibration effectiveness and efficiency. In addition, through closed-book question answering, we find that the calibrated PLM possesses knowledge generalization ability after finetuning.Beyond the calibration performance, we further investigate and visualize the knowledge calibration mechanism.

papers.title: Finding Universal Grammatical Relations in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: To what extent does Multilingual BERT learn a cross-lingual representation of syntactic structure? Does mBERT learn universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations; its syntactic subspaces are shared across languages and capture dependency clusters that largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, indicating the model induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT learns cross-lingual syntactic representations and induces universal grammatical relations without explicit supervision, which largely agree with the dependency labels of Universal Dependencies.
papers.key_findings:
The structural probe recovers syntactic tree distances in multiple languages from mBERT representations.
The syntactic subspaces are shared across languages, enabling zero-shot cross-lingual transfer of syntactic information.
mBERT represents dependency clusters that largely overlap with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy, showing it learns universal grammatical relations.
The cross-lingual syntactic subspace is a small part (approx. 32-128 dimensions) of the overall 768-dimensional representation.
Transfer probe performance is substantially correlated with subspace similarity across languages.
papers.limitation:
Cannot tease apart whether transfer performance is caused by subword overlap or by a more fundamental sharing of parameters.
Only conduct a qualitative study in the unsupervised emergence of dependency labels via t-SNE; future work could extend to quantitative results.
Acknowledge issues in interpreting t-SNE plots.
Methods cannot support causal implications for the decisions made by the model.
future_direction: Explore other multilingual models like XLM and XLM-RoBERTa.
Attempt to understand the extent to which the discovered properties have causal implications for the model's decisions.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found evidence that Multilingual BERT (mBERT), a transformer-based multilingual masked language model, is capable of zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that some aspects of its representations are shared cross-lingually. To better understand this overlap, we extend recent work on finding syntactic trees in neural networks' internal representations to the multilingual setting. We show that subspaces of mBERT representations recover syntactic tree distances in languages other than English, and that these subspaces are approximately shared across languages. Motivated by these results, we present an unsupervised analysis method that provides evidence mBERT learns representations of syntactic dependency labels, in the form of clusters which largely agree with the Universal Dependencies taxonomy. This evidence suggests that even without explicit supervision, multilingual masked language models learn certain linguistic universals.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Discovering Salient Neurons in Deep NLP Models
papers.research_question: Can we identify subsets of neurons that learn specific linguistic properties, and how is linguistic knowledge localized, distributed, and affected by fine-tuning in NLP models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Linguistic Correlation Analysis (LCA) for extracting salient neurons in NLP models, revealing that linguistic knowledge is localized in lower layers for basic properties and distributed in higher layers for complex concepts, with variations across models and during fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: The LCA method provides insights into how linguistic knowledge is encoded in neurons, showing localization patterns and redistribution during fine-tuning, with implications for model understanding and transfer learning.
papers.key_findings:
Small subsets of neurons can predict different linguistic tasks.
Neurons for basic lexical information are localized in lower layers, while those for complex concepts are in higher layers.
Linguistic information is redundantly preserved across neurons.
During transfer learning, salient linguistic neurons relocate to lower layers in some models like RoBERTa and XLNet.
Multilingual models exhibit similar neuron distribution for concepts across different languages.
future_direction: Pinpointing specific concepts regressed to lower layers versus those retained in higher layers during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: While a lot of work has been done in understanding representations learned within deep NLP models and what knowledge they capture, little attention has been paid towards individual neurons. We present a technique called as Linguistic Correlation Analysis to extract salient neurons in the model, with respect to any extrinsic property - with the goal of understanding how such a knowledge is preserved within neurons. We carry out a fine-grained analysis to answer the following questions: (i) can we identify subsets of neurons in the network that capture specific linguistic properties? (ii) how localized or distributed neurons are across the network? iii) how redundantly is the information preserved? iv) how fine-tuning pre-trained models towards downstream NLP tasks, impacts the learned linguistic knowledge? iv) how do architectures vary in learning different linguistic properties? Our data-driven, quantitative analysis illuminates interesting findings: (i) we found small subsets of neurons that can predict different linguistic tasks, ii) with neurons capturing basic lexical information (such as suffixation) localized in lower most layers, iii) while those learning complex concepts (such as syntactic role) predominantly in middle and higher layers, iii) that salient linguistic neurons are relocated from higher to lower layers during transfer learning, as the network preserve the higher layers for task specific information, iv) we found interesting differences across pre-trained models, with respect to how linguistic information is preserved within, and v) we found that concept exhibit similar neuron distribution across different languages in the multilingual transformer models. Our code is publicly available as part of the NeuroX toolkit.

papers.title: When Less Language is More: Language-Reasoning Disentanglement Makes LLMs Better Multilingual Reasoners
papers.research_question: Can reasoning and language processing in LLMs be disentangled to improve multilingual reasoning performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning and language can be disentangled in LLMs by ablating language-specific components in hidden states, leading to improved multilingual reasoning performance across diverse models and languages.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that language and reasoning are separable in LLMs, and the proposed training-free intervention provides a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Language-reasoning disentanglement via activation ablation consistently improves multilingual reasoning performance across 10 open-weight LLMs and 11 typologically diverse languages.
There is a negative correlation between language-specific activation and reasoning accuracy; removing language-specific signals improves reasoning.
Middle layers are most effective for disentanglement, improving reasoning while preserving language fidelity, whereas upper-layer ablation degrades output fluency.
The training-free intervention achieves comparable or superior results to post-training methods like supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
Low-resource languages show a trade-off: reasoning improves with ablation, but language fidelity drops more sharply than in high-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
After ablation, models tend to default to English, which may reduce language fidelity, especially for low-resource languages.
The exact ratios of pretraining data for different languages are unknown, which limits a definitive explanation of the convergence phenomenon.
future_direction: Further investigation into the convergence of non-English representations to English after ablation.
Exploring adaptive ablation strategies to balance reasoning improvement and language fluency for low-resource languages.
Combining the training-free intervention with post-training methods for enhanced multilingual reasoning.
papers.abstract: Multilingual reasoning remains a significant challenge for large language models (LLMs), with performance disproportionately favoring high-resource languages. Drawing inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human reasoning functions largely independently of language processing, we hypothesize that LLMs similarly encode reasoning and language as separable components that can be disentangled to enhance multilingual reasoning. To evaluate this, we perform a causal intervention by ablating language-specific representations at inference time. Experiments on 10 open-weight LLMs spanning 11 typologically diverse languages show that this language-specific ablation consistently boosts multilingual reasoning performance. Layer-wise analyses further confirm that language and reasoning representations can be effectively disentangled throughout the model, yielding improved multilingual reasoning capabilities, while preserving top-layer language features remains essential for maintaining linguistic fidelity. Compared to post-training methods such as supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning, our training-free language-reasoning disentanglement achieves comparable or superior results with minimal computational overhead. These findings shed light on the internal mechanisms underlying multilingual reasoning in LLMs and suggest a lightweight and interpretable strategy for improving cross-lingual generalization.

papers.title: Linguistic Minimal Pairs Elicit Linguistic Similarity in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Large Language Models represent different linguistic phenomena, and are linguistically similar phenomena represented similarly in LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method using linguistic minimal pairs to measure linguistic similarity in LLMs, revealing that linguistic similarity is influenced by training data, aligns with fine-grained linguistic categories, weakly correlates with semantic similarity, and shows limited cross-lingual alignment.
papers.conclusion: The work provides insights into LLMs' internal language processing, bridging neural models and linguistic theory, and offers a foundation for future research.
papers.key_findings:
Linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages.
Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones.
Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, indicating its context-dependent nature.
LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Dependent on the quality and scope of existing linguistic minimal pair datasets
Limited to three languages, not representing global linguistic diversity
Only captures a fraction of language's complexity with 150 phenomena
future_direction: Developing more high-quality minimal pairs
Broadening language coverage to include more diverse linguistic families
Increasing the range of phenomena studied
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel analysis that leverages linguistic minimal pairs to probe the internal linguistic representations of Large Language Models (LLMs). By measuring the similarity between LLM activation differences across minimal pairs, we quantify the and gain insight into the linguistic knowledge captured by LLMs. Our large-scale experiments, spanning 100+ LLMs and 150k minimal pairs in three languages, reveal properties of linguistic similarity from four key aspects: consistency across LLMs, relation to theoretical categorizations, dependency to semantic context, and cross-lingual alignment of relevant phenomena. Our findings suggest that 1) linguistic similarity is significantly influenced by training data exposure, leading to higher cross-LLM agreement in higher-resource languages. 2) Linguistic similarity strongly aligns with fine-grained theoretical linguistic categories but weakly with broader ones. 3) Linguistic similarity shows a weak correlation with semantic similarity, showing its context-dependent nature. 4) LLMs exhibit limited cross-lingual alignment in their understanding of relevant linguistic phenomena. This work demonstrates the potential of minimal pairs as a window into the neural representations of language in LLMs, shedding light on the relationship between LLMs and linguistic theory. Codes and data are available at https://github.com/ChenDelong1999/Linguistic-Similarity

papers.title: A Study of Cross-Lingual Ability and Language-specific Information in Multilingual BERT
papers.research_question: What factors influence the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT, and does language-specific information exist in its representations?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies datasize and context window size as crucial factors for cross-lingual transferability in multilingual BERT, and introduces Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to manipulate language-specific information for unsupervised token translation and improved cross-lingual transfer.
papers.conclusion: The cross-lingual ability of m-BERT is learned from longer dependency and requires a massive amount of data; language-specific information can be manipulated via simple shifts to improve cross-lingual transfer, opening a new direction for strengthening cross-lingual ability.
papers.key_findings:
With small pretraining data, BERT does not outperform non-contextualized embeddings in cross-lingual ability; with large data, BERT achieves superior cross-lingual alignment.
Breaking down long dependency (smaller window size) hurts cross-lingual ability when pretraining data is large, but helps when data is small.
Language-specific information exists in m-BERT representations and can be extracted via mean difference vectors.
Applying Mean Difference Shift (MDS) to hidden representations can control the output language of m-BERT, enabling unsupervised token translation.
Using MDS to shift representations improves cross-lingual transfer performance on XNLI for most languages, except those with high subword overlap with English.
papers.limitation:
MDS does not improve performance for languages with high subword overlap with English (e.g., Spanish, French) due to shared subwords having different meanings, indicating the need for a more delicate mechanism.
The quality of unsupervised translation using MDS is not acceptable; only token conversion rate is measured, not fluency or accuracy.
future_direction: Develop a more delicate mechanism for applying language-specific shifts that considers differences among vocabularies.
papers.abstract: Recently, multilingual BERT works remarkably well on cross-lingual transfer tasks, superior to static non-contextualized word embeddings. In this work, we provide an in-depth experimental study to supplement the existing literature of cross-lingual ability. We compare the cross-lingual ability of non-contextualized and contextualized representation model with the same data. We found that datasize and context window size are crucial factors to the transferability. We also observe the language-specific information in multilingual BERT. By manipulating the latent representations, we can control the output languages of multilingual BERT, and achieve unsupervised token translation. We further show that based on the observation, there is a computationally cheap but effective approach to improve the cross-lingual ability of multilingual BERT.

papers.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
papers.research_question: What is the role of induction heads in few-shot in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides empirical evidence that induction heads, through their prefix matching and copying mechanism, are a fundamental component enabling few-shot in-context learning in large language models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads are a fundamental mechanism underlying in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Ablating a small percentage (1-3%) of induction heads leads to substantial decreases in ICL performance, much more so than ablating random heads.
Blocking the specific induction attention pattern (via attention knockout) causes performance drops similar to full head ablation, confirming the mechanism's specific role.
The importance of induction heads for ICL holds across abstract pattern recognition tasks and real-world NLP tasks.
Induction heads utilize a 'fuzzy' version of the prefix matching and copying mechanism to enable pattern matching in ICL.
The ablation of induction heads affects few-shot performance more severely than zero-shot performance, highlighting their role in learning from examples.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on prefix-matching scores as a proxy for identifying induction heads, lacking a mechanistic basis for definitive identification.
Attention knockout experiments are confined to abstract-pattern recognition tasks; further research is required for NLP tasks.
The experiments do not test whether induction heads are the only computational process contributing to ICL; other mechanisms may exist.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown a remarkable ability to learn and perform complex tasks through in-context learning (ICL). However, a comprehensive understanding of its internal mechanisms is still lacking. This paper explores the role of induction heads in a few-shot ICL setting. We analyse two state-of-the-art models, Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B on abstract pattern recognition and NLP tasks. Our results show that even a minimal ablation of induction heads leads to ICL performance decreases of up to ~32% for abstract pattern recognition tasks, bringing the performance close to random. For NLP tasks, this ablation substantially decreases the model's ability to benefit from examples, bringing few-shot ICL performance close to that of zero-shot prompts. We further use attention knockout to disable specific induction patterns, and present fine-grained evidence for the role that the induction mechanism plays in ICL.

papers.title: Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers: A cross-lingual exploration of knowledge
papers.research_question: This study examines the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and investigates the role of attention mechanisms in this process.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes MEMAT, a knowledge editing method that modifies attention heads in addition to MLP layers, leading to improved performance, cross-lingual portability, and enhanced model understanding of edited facts.
papers.conclusion: MEMAT improves knowledge editing by leveraging attention heads, demonstrating portability and effectiveness across languages, and enhancing the model's understanding of the inserted factual associations.
papers.key_findings:
MEMIT's cross-lingual performance is dependent on subject tokenization similarity between languages.
Attention heads encode language-independent information about factual associations, achieving high accuracy in classifying truthful sentences.
MEMAT outperforms MEMIT across all evaluation metrics (success and magnitude), with improvements exceeding 10% in some cases.
The attention head corrections learned by MEMAT are portable and can be recycled for editing new sets of factual triplets.
MEMAT enhances the model's comprehension of the edited knowledge rather than merely reintroducing it, as evidenced by improved paraphrase and neighborhood metrics.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to English and Catalan; generalization to other linguistic contexts may be limited due to alphabet similarity.
Broader challenges in knowledge editing persist, such as the inability to modify related knowledge and lack of bidirectionality.
future_direction: Investigating language adaptation techniques to enable models to perform tasks in a more language-agnostic manner.
Exploring the role that each architecture component plays in alternative domains to enhance explainable AI.
papers.abstract: Recent research has explored methods for updating and modifying factual knowledge in large language models, often focusing on specific multi-layer perceptron blocks. This study expands on this work by examining the effectiveness of existing knowledge editing methods across languages and delving into the role of attention mechanisms in this process. Drawing from the insights gained, we propose Mass-Editing Memory with Attention in Transformers (MEMAT), a method that achieves significant improvements in all metrics while requiring minimal parameter modifications. MEMAT delivers a remarkable 10% increase in magnitude metrics, benefits languages not included in the training data and also demonstrates a high degree of portability. Our code and data are at https://github.com/dtamayo-nlp/MEMAT.

papers.title: Toward a Theory of Generalizability in LLM Mechanistic Interpretability Research
papers.research_question: What principles justify extrapolating mechanistic claims from one LLM to another, and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a theoretical framework (axes of correspondence) for generalizability in mechanistic interpretability and validates it with an empirical study on 1-back attention heads in Pythia models.
papers.conclusion: Progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
1-back attention heads show strong developmental consistency across random seeds and model sizes, but limited positional consistency.
Larger models show earlier onset, steeper slope, and higher peak of 1-back attention.
Developmental trajectories of 1-back attention are highly correlated across random seeds of the same model, and also across models of different sizes.
papers.limitation:
The theoretical framework is preliminary and may require refinement.
The empirical study is limited to a specific mechanism (1-back attention) and a single model family (Pythia).
future_direction: Building a theoretically legible typology (or 'phylogeny') of model instances that predicts which pairs will share similar mechanisms.
Expanding the framework to other axes of correspondence and mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Research on Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly focuses on identifying mechanistic explanations for their behaviors, yet the field lacks clear principles for determining when (and how) findings from one model instance generalize to another. This paper addresses a fundamental epistemological challenge: given a mechanistic claim about a particular model, what justifies extrapolating this finding to other LLMs -- and along which dimensions might such generalizations hold? I propose five potential axes of correspondence along which mechanistic claims might generalize, including: functional (whether they satisfy the same functional criteria), developmental (whether they develop at similar points during pretraining), positional (whether they occupy similar absolute or relative positions), relational (whether they interact with other model components in similar ways), and configurational (whether they correspond to particular regions or structures in weight-space). To empirically validate this framework, I analyze "1-back attention heads" (components attending to previous tokens) across pretraining in random seeds of the Pythia models (14M, 70M, 160M, 410M). The results reveal striking consistency in the developmental trajectories of 1-back attention across models, while positional consistency is more limited. Moreover, seeds of larger models systematically show earlier onsets, steeper slopes, and higher peaks of 1-back attention. I also address possible objections to the arguments and proposals outlined here. Finally, I conclude by arguing that progress on the generalizability of mechanistic interpretability research will consist in mapping constitutive design properties of LLMs to their emergent behaviors and mechanisms.

papers.title: Inferring the nature of linguistic computations in the brain
papers.research_question: How can we infer the nature of linguistic computations from neural data, and what are the pitfalls in interpreting such data and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that neural data alone is insufficient to infer the computational mechanisms of sentence processing, and that models must be evaluated based on cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles to be explanatory.
papers.conclusion: Computational modeling is vital for understanding sentence processing, but models must compute linguistically-sufficient representations via explicit cognitive operations and stay faithful to neurophysiological principles, and should not be judged solely on predictive power.
papers.key_findings:
The presence of a 1-2-4 Hz pattern in neural data does not necessarily imply hierarchical processing; it can also arise from associative models.
Artificial neural networks can produce the 1-2-4 Hz pattern without explicit sentence structure, but this does not rule out hierarchical processing in the brain.
Predictive power of a model is not the sole criterion for explaining brain function; models must also be faithful to cognitive and neural principles.
The amount of training data used in ANNs may not reflect the brain's learning environment, and rule-based models might be more explanatory in some cases.
Statistical models are not necessarily more parsimonious than hierarchical models, as they may require extensive training and latent syntactic information.
future_direction: Using naturalistic paradigms to study language processing
Integrating multiple data sources (e.g., EEG, fMRI) to test models
Developing models that are explicit about cognitive operations and neurophysiological implementation
papers.abstract: Sentences contain structure that determines their meaning beyond that of individual words. An influential study by Ding and colleagues (2016) used frequency tagging of phrases and sentences to show that the human brain is sensitive to structure by finding peaks of neural power at the rate at which structures were presented. Since then, there has been a rich debate on how to best explain this pattern of results with profound impact on the language sciences. Models that use hierarchical structure building, as well as models based on associative sequence processing, can predict the neural response, creating an inferential impasse as to which class of models explains the nature of the linguistic computations reflected in the neural readout. In the current manuscript, we discuss pitfalls and common fallacies seen in the conclusions drawn in the literature illustrated by various simulations. We conclude that inferring the neural operations of sentence processing based on these neural data, and any like it, alone, is insufficient. We discuss how to best evaluate models and how to approach the modeling of neural readouts to sentence processing in a manner that remains faithful to cognitive, neural, and linguistic principles.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Unraveling Babel: Exploring Multilingual Activation Patterns of LLMs and Their Applications
papers.research_question: How do the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs differ when processing different languages, and how can these patterns be leveraged for applications like model pruning?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures to study multilingual activation patterns, and uses these patterns to guide language-specific model pruning, reducing computation while maintaining or even improving performance.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals multilingual activation patterns in LLMs, their connections to language families and instruction tuning, and provides a new effective approach for model pruning and sparse activation.
papers.key_findings:
Activation patterns differ across languages and correlate with language families and genera.
Multilingual shared experts are concentrated in middle layers, while shallow and deep layers contain more language-specific experts.
Instruction tuning significantly alters activation patterns, with the largest changes in the last layer.
Pruning based on expert activation frequency outperforms random pruning and can exceed the performance of the original unpruned model in some languages.
Different layers exhibit different activation sparsity, so configuring layer-specific pruning rates yields better results.
papers.limitation:
The pruning ratio is limited due to low activation sparsity in most layers of models like Llama 2.
There is a concern that simplified representations may fail to capture the model's out-of-distribution behavior, though evaluation on out-of-distribution tasks provides some mitigation.
future_direction: Extend experiments to a broader array of models and languages.
Explore how to further leverage these insights to utilize and enhance the multilingual capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Recently, large language models (LLMs) have achieved tremendous breakthroughs in the field of NLP, but still lack understanding of their internal neuron activities when processing different languages. We designed a method to convert dense LLMs into fine-grained MoE architectures, and then visually studied the multilingual activation patterns of LLMs through expert activation frequency heatmaps. Through comprehensive experiments on different model families, different model sizes, and different variants, we analyzed the similarities and differences in the internal neuron activation patterns of LLMs when processing different languages. Specifically, we investigated the distribution of high-frequency activated experts, multilingual shared experts, whether multilingual activation patterns are related to language families, and the impact of instruction tuning on activation patterns. We further explored leveraging the discovered differences in expert activation frequencies to guide sparse activation and pruning. Experimental results demonstrated that our method significantly outperformed random expert pruning and even exceeded the performance of unpruned models in some languages. Additionally, we found that configuring different pruning rates for different layers based on activation level differences could achieve better results. Our findings reveal the multilingual processing mechanisms within LLMs and utilize these insights to offer new perspectives for applications such as sparse activation and model pruning.

papers.title: Inferring Functionality of Attention Heads from their Parameters
papers.research_question: How to infer the functionality of attention heads in LLMs from their parameters without model training or inference, and to map how strongly heads implement predefined operations or to infer salient operations of a given head.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MAPS, a framework to infer attention head functionality directly from parameters, enabling mapping of predefined operations across heads and automatic characterization of salient operations.
papers.conclusion: Introduces MAPS, an efficient framework for inferring attention heads’ functionality from their parameters, and showcases its utility in systematically mapping functionality across the model and automatically characterizing salient operations of a given head.
papers.key_findings:
MAPS estimations correlate with head outputs during inference and are causally linked to model predictions.
MAPS reveals attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies.
MAPS provides insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs.
Automatic pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment.
Heads often implement multiple relations, and smaller models tend to encode more relations per head.
papers.limitation: The automatic description pipeline sometimes hallucinates patterns not present in the mappings.
future_direction: Improve the automatic description pipeline to reduce hallucinations by using confidence aggregation, intrinsic classifiers, or NLI models.
papers.abstract: Attention heads are one of the building blocks of large language models (LLMs). Prior work on investigating their operation mostly focused on analyzing their behavior during inference for specific circuits or tasks. In this work, we seek a comprehensive mapping of the operations they implement in a model. We propose MAPS (Mapping Attention head ParameterS), an efficient framework that infers the functionality of attention heads from their parameters, without any model training or inference. We showcase the utility of MAPS for answering two types of questions: (a) given a predefined operation, mapping how strongly heads across the model implement it, and (b) given an attention head, inferring its salient functionality. Evaluating MAPS on 20 operations across 6 popular LLMs shows its estimations correlate with the head's outputs during inference and are causally linked to the model's predictions. Moreover, its mappings reveal attention heads of certain operations that were overlooked in previous studies, and valuable insights on function universality and architecture biases in LLMs. Next, we present an automatic pipeline and analysis that leverage MAPS to characterize the salient operations of a given head. Our pipeline produces plausible operation descriptions for most heads, as assessed by human judgment, while revealing diverse operations.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Position-aware Automatic Circuit Discovery
papers.research_question: How can we incorporate positional information into automatic circuit discovery for language models to address limitations of position-agnostic methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces position-aware circuit discovery (PEAP) and dataset schemas to enable fully automated discovery of position-sensitive circuits, achieving better faithfulness than position-agnostic methods.
papers.conclusion: Position-aware circuit discovery and schemas improve circuit faithfulness and enable automated analysis of variable-length inputs, providing a more precise foundation for mechanistic explanations.
papers.key_findings:
Position-aware circuits are smaller and more faithful than position-agnostic circuits.
Automatically generated schemas (with or without saliency masks) yield circuits comparable to those from human-designed schemas.
The proposed method handles variable-length inputs via schemas, enabling circuit discovery in more naturalistic settings.
papers.limitation:
Schemas assume sequential order of spans, which may not hold for all datasets.
The schema generation and application pipeline may not always produce valid schemas for all examples.
future_direction: Relax the sequential order assumption in schemas to support greater variation across examples.
Investigate the components in the circuit for the Winobias task to understand the balance between task-relevant and bias-inducing factors.

papers.title: Identifying a Circuit for Verb Conjugation in GPT-2
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 perform subject-verb agreement, and what is the minimal circuit responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a minimal circuit of attention heads in GPT-2 Small responsible for subject-verb agreement, showing that basic agreement relies on a small subset of heads while more complex linguistic features require larger circuits.
papers.conclusion: The study successfully isolated a circuit for verb conjugation in GPT-2, demonstrating that basic syntactic processing relies on a small subset of attention heads, but more complex linguistic features require larger, more distributed circuits.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-2 achieves high accuracy on subject-verb agreement across a range of controlled linguistic settings, including plural, negation, prefix, pronoun, tense, and irregular verbs.
A minimal circuit of 12 attention heads can achieve near-full model performance (0.65 accuracy vs. 0.70) on the base singular subject task.
For settings like plural, negation, and pronoun, circuit performance remains poor even after modest expansions, suggesting these features are more diffusely encoded or rely on non-attention mechanisms.
For settings like prefix, past tense, and irregular verbs, larger circuit expansions (up to 97 heads) achieve closer to full model performance (e.g., 0.82 vs. 0.93 for irregular verbs).
Analysis of attention patterns reveals categories of head functions, such as primary subject-anchors and conjunction-tracking, with some heads consistently important across settings.
papers.limitation:
Greedy search strategy may miss optimal circuits and combinatorial interactions.
Analysis focused exclusively on attention heads, omitting MLP components.
Path patching with resample ablation may still introduce unrealistic activation patterns.
Linguistic settings are bounded and artificial, not covering real-world complexity.
Manual categorization of head functions introduces subjectivity and limits reproducibility.
future_direction: MLP integration
Global optimization methods (e.g., ACDC) for circuit discovery
Cross-model comparisons to generalize findings
papers.abstract: I implement a procedure to isolate and interpret the sub-network (or "circuit") responsible for subject-verb agreement in GPT-2 Small. In this study, the model is given prompts where the subject is either singular (e.g. "Alice") or plural (e.g. "Alice and Bob"), and the task is to correctly predict the appropriate verb form ("walks" for singular subjects, "walk" for plural subjects). Using a series of techniques-including performance verification automatic circuit discovery via direct path patching, and direct logit attribution- I isolate a candidate circuit that contributes significantly to the model's correct verb conjugation. The results suggest that only a small fraction of the network's component-token pairs is needed to achieve near-model performance on the base task but substantially more for more complex settings.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: LinguaLens: Towards Interpreting Linguistic Mechanisms of Large Language Models via Sparse Auto-Encoder
papers.research_question: Can we identify the minimal components within an LLM responsible for specific linguistic processing abilities? Can we comprehensively model the internal linguistic functionalities of the model?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes LINGUALENS, a framework using Sparse Auto-Encoders to interpret linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, revealing intrinsic representations of linguistic knowledge, cross-layer and cross-lingual distribution patterns, and enabling control of model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LINGUALENS provides a systematic framework for interpreting linguistic mechanisms in LLMs, showing that they encode structured linguistic knowledge and enabling more interpretable and controllable language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
LINGUALENS effectively identifies linguistic features in SAE space, with metrics like FRC showing strong correlations.
Linguistic functions distribute across layers in stages: morphology and syntax in lower layers, pragmatics in middle layers, and deep semantics in upper layers.
Cross-lingual analysis shows higher overlap for semantic and pragmatic features than morphological and syntactic ones, indicating shared representations.
Interventions on SAE features (ablation and enhancement) demonstrate causal effects on model outputs, validated by LLM judges.
Deep semantics processing, such as reference resolution and metaphor interpretation, activates specific base vectors in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Dataset size is limited to approximately 50 sentence pairs per linguistic feature.
Feature count is 145, which is not comprehensive for all linguistic phenomena.
Experiments are conducted only on Llama-3.1-8B due to computational constraints.
Intervention effects are less stable and efficacious compared to conventional fine-tuning techniques.
future_direction: Expand the dataset to include more linguistic features and sentences.
Apply the framework to a wider variety of model architectures and larger models.
Refine SAE-based intervention methods for better efficacy and stability.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate exceptional performance on tasks requiring complex linguistic abilities, such as reference disambiguation and metaphor recognition/generation. Although LLMs possess impressive capabilities, their internal mechanisms for processing and representing linguistic knowledge remain largely opaque. Prior research on linguistic mechanisms is limited by coarse granularity, limited analysis scale, and narrow focus.
