This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: Training Dynamics of Contextual N-Grams in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do contextual n-gram circuits form during training? Do they form gradually or in a sudden phase transition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that contextual n-gram circuits form gradually as second-order circuits, combining pre-existing n-gram and language detection circuits, contrary to the hypothesis that circuits form in sudden phase transitions.
papers.conclusion: The formation of the contextual n-gram circuit is gradual and represents a second-order circuit, adding complexity to the quantization model of neural scaling.
papers.key_findings:
The German context neuron and German trigram prediction are learned early in a phase transition, but the trigram prediction does not depend on the context neuron initially.
The contextual n-gram circuit (where trigram prediction depends on the context neuron) forms gradually later in training.
There is a large cohort of context neurons that form early but are quickly unlearned, and most have low impact on loss.
The direct effect of the context neuron boosts German unigrams, and the indirect effect enables contextual n-grams.
The general phase transition in capabilities coincides with the learning rate warm-up.
papers.limitation: The analysis focused on specifically selected n-grams that strongly rely on the German context neuron, and it is uncertain whether the neuron contributes to other circuits.
future_direction: Fully reverse-engineer the role of context neurons in language models by comprehensively identifying all circuits they are involved in or proving that unigram and n-gram effects are sufficient to explain their effects.
Investigate the emergence and role of the early context neurons that form and are quickly unlearned.
papers.abstract: Prior work has shown the existence of contextual neurons in language models, including a neuron that activates on German text. We show that this neuron exists within a broader contextual n-gram circuit: we find late layer neurons which recognize and continue n-grams common in German text, but which only activate if the German neuron is active. We investigate the formation of this circuit throughout training and find that it is an example of what we call a second-order circuit. In particular, both the constituent n-gram circuits and the German detection circuit which culminates in the German neuron form with independent functions early in training - the German detection circuit partially through modeling German unigram statistics, and the n-grams by boosting appropriate completions. Only after both circuits have already formed do they fit together into a second-order circuit. Contrary to the hypotheses presented in prior work, we find that the contextual n-gram circuit forms gradually rather than in a sudden phase transition. We further present a range of anomalous observations such as a simultaneous phase transition in many tasks coinciding with the learning rate warm-up, and evidence that many context neurons form simultaneously early in training but are later unlearned.

papers.title: Are formal and functional linguistic mechanisms dissociated in language models?
papers.research_question: Do current large language models exhibit distinct localization (dissociation) of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms in their internal circuits?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds evidence for formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness (formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than functional ones, and vice-versa), but not in terms of circuit overlap, suggesting a shared pool of mechanisms for formal tasks rather than a single unified region.
papers.conclusion: There is evidence for emerging formal-functional dissociation in LLMs in terms of cross-task faithfulness, but not in terms of circuit overlap, indicating a set of shared formal linguistic mechanisms rather than a single unified region.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for formal and functional linguistic tasks have low overlap (IoU).
Circuits for formal tasks do not have especially high overlap with each other, arguing against a single unified formal network.
Formal task circuits perform other formal tasks better than they perform functional tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Functional task circuits perform other functional tasks better than they perform formal tasks (cross-task faithfulness).
Clustering based on cross-task faithfulness vectors separates formal and functional tasks into distinct groups.
papers.limitation: The circuit-finding method (EAP-IG) may not perfectly capture all relevant mechanisms, and the findings are limited to the specific models and tasks studied.
future_direction: Studying more models and tasks to generalize findings.
Using more granular analyses (e.g., neuron-level, sparse feature circuits).
Investigating the effects of model scale and architecture on dissociation.
papers.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable, these capabilities are unevenly distributed: they excel at formal linguistic tasks, such as producing fluent, grammatical text, but struggle more with functional linguistic tasks like reasoning and consistent fact retrieval. Inspired by neuroscience, recent work suggests that to succeed on both formal and functional linguistic tasks, LLMs should use different mechanisms for each; such localization could either be built-in or emerge spontaneously through training. In this paper, we ask: do current models, with fast-improving functional linguistic abilities, exhibit distinct localization of formal and functional linguistic mechanisms? We answer this by finding and comparing the "circuits", or minimal computational subgraphs, responsible for various formal and functional tasks. Comparing 5 LLMs across 10 distinct tasks, we find that while there is indeed little overlap between circuits for formal and functional tasks, there is also little overlap between formal linguistic tasks, as exists in the human brain. Thus, a single formal linguistic network, unified and distinct from functional task circuits, remains elusive. However, in terms of cross-task faithfulness - the ability of one circuit to solve another's task - we observe a separation between formal and functional mechanisms, suggesting that shared mechanisms between formal tasks may exist.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: Tracing Facts or just Copies? A critical investigation of the Competitions of Mechanisms in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in LLMs mediate the competition between factual recall from parametric memory and counterfactual information provided in context? Do they perform selective counterfactual suppression or general copy suppression, and are they domain-specific?
papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: Mechanistic Understanding and Mitigation of Language Confusion in English-Centric Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does language confusion arise mechanistically in English-centric LLMs, and can it be mitigated through neuron-level interventions?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first mechanistic interpretability study of language confusion in LLMs, revealing that confusion points arise from transition failures in final layers and can be effectively mitigated by editing a small set of critical neurons identified through comparative analysis.
papers.conclusion: This work provides the first mechanistic interpretability account of language confusion in English-centric LLMs, demonstrating that targeted neuron editing can robustly mitigate confusion without sacrificing general competence or fluency.
papers.key_findings:
Confusion points are critical drivers of language confusion, and token replacement at these points reduces confusion.
Layer-wise analysis shows that language confusion is caused by failed transitions to the target language in the final layers.
Neuron-level analysis identifies specific FFN neurons in late layers that are responsible for confusion points.
Comparative importance selection of neurons enables effective mitigation of language confusion through editing.
Neuron editing achieves confusion reduction comparable to multilingual tuning for many languages while preserving general competence and output quality.
papers.limitation:
Analysis primarily focuses on the monolingual setting; cross-lingual contexts are left for future research.
Neuron editing interventions may require further validation across broader domains and model architectures.
Fully understanding how these mechanisms interact with other multilingual phenomena warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Extending analysis to cross-lingual contexts
Validating neuron editing across broader domains and model architectures
Investigating interactions with other multilingual phenomena
papers.abstract: Language confusion -- where large language models (LLMs) generate unintended languages against the user's need -- remains a critical challenge, especially for English-centric models. We present the first mechanistic interpretability (MI) study of language confusion, combining behavioral benchmarking with neuron-level analysis. Using the Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB), we show that confusion points (CPs) -- specific positions where language switches occur -- are central to this phenomenon. Through layer-wise analysis with TunedLens and targeted neuron attribution, we reveal that transition failures in the final layers drive confusion. We further demonstrate that editing a small set of critical neurons, identified via comparative analysis with a multilingual-tuned counterpart, substantially mitigates confusion while largely preserving general competence and fluency. Our approach matches multilingual alignment in confusion reduction for many languages and yields cleaner, higher-quality outputs. These findings provide new insights into the internal dynamics of LLMs and highlight neuron-level interventions as a promising direction for robust, interpretable multilingual language modeling. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/ercong21/lang_confusion.

papers.title: Negative Pre-activations Differentiate Syntax
papers.research_question: Whether and how negative pre-activations are leveraged by models, specifically for syntactic processing.
papers.core_contribution: Negative pre-activations in a sparse subpopulation of Wasserstein neurons are actively used as a substrate for syntax in smooth-activation language models.
papers.conclusion: Negative pre-activations are not an inert byproduct but a functional substrate that certain neurons leverage to implement grammar, reframing ReLU-era intuitions.
papers.key_findings:
Wasserstein neurons, which have non-Gaussian pre-activation distributions, emerge early in training and track grammatical competence.
Zeroing negative pre-activations of top Wasserstein neurons disproportionately increases perplexity and degrades grammatical performance on BLiMP and TSE, while random or perplexity-matched ablations of non-Wasserstein neurons do not.
The same ablation has a milder effect on non-grammatical benchmarks, showing a double dissociation between syntax and other capabilities.
Layerwise ablations reveal that early layers are most critical for grammar, and damage compounds across depth.
Wasserstein neurons implement 'negative differentiation', mapping similar inputs (e.g., syntactic tokens) to distinct negative pre-activation values.
papers.limitation: The ablation method zeroing negative pre-activations disproportionately collapses negative-negative pairs, so correlations between negative-negative pair prevalence and grammatical vulnerability may partly reflect the intervention mechanics.
papers.abstract: A recently discovered class of entangled neurons, known as Wasserstein neurons, is disproportionately critical in large language models despite constituting only a very small fraction of the network: their targeted removal collapses the model, consistent with their unique role in differentiating similar inputs. Interestingly, in Wasserstein neurons immediately preceding smooth activation functions, such differentiation manifests in the negative pre-activation space, especially in early layers. Pairs of similar inputs are driven to highly distinct negative values, and these pairs involve syntactic tokens such as determiners and prepositions. We show that this negative region is functional rather than simply favorable for optimization. A minimal, sign-specific intervention that zeroes only the negative pre-activations of a small subset of entangled neurons significantly weakens overall model function and disrupts grammatical behavior, while both random and perplexity-matched controls leave grammatical performance largely unchanged. Part of speech analysis localizes the excess surprisal to syntactic scaffolding tokens, and layer-specific interventions reveal that small local degradations accumulate across depth. Over training checkpoints, the same ablation impairs grammatical behavior as Wasserstein neurons emerge and stabilize. Together, these results identify negative differentiation in a sparse subset of entangled neurons as a crucial mechanism that language models rely on for syntax.

papers.title: From Neurons to Semantics: Evaluating Cross-Linguistic Alignment Capabilities of Large Language Models via Neurons Alignment
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the cross-lingual alignment capabilities of large language models in a semantically grounded way?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes NeuronXA, a neuron state-based method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, which shows strong correlation with downstream task performance and transferability.
papers.conclusion: NeuronXA provides a robust and semantically grounded method for evaluating cross-lingual alignment in LLMs, with strong correlations to downstream performance, and has potential for advancing multilingual model research.
papers.key_findings:
Neuron state-based representation more effectively encodes cross-lingual knowledge and improves semantic retrieval accuracy.
NeuronXA achieves high Pearson correlation with downstream tasks (0.9556) and transferability (0.8514).
Alignment scores are highest in middle layers, lower in bottom and top layers, indicating that middle layers contain shared multilingual neurons.
NAS representation reduces directional asymmetry in retrieval tasks.
NeuronXA is robust and generalizable across different base languages and datasets.
papers.limitation:
NeuronXA requires access to the model's intrinsic representations, so it cannot be directly applied to closed-source models.
NeuronXA cannot encompass all perspectives on model capabilities.
future_direction: Extending NeuronXA to evaluate other model capabilities
Applying NeuronXA to expand models to underrepresented languages
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable multilingual capabilities, however, how to evaluate cross-lingual alignment remains underexplored. Existing alignment benchmarks primarily focus on sentence embeddings, but prior research has shown that neural models tend to induce a non-smooth representation space, which impact of semantic alignment evaluation on low-resource languages. Inspired by neuroscientific findings that similar information activates overlapping neuronal regions, we propose a novel Neuron State-Based Cross-Lingual Alignment (NeuronXA) to assess the cross-lingual a lignment capabilities of LLMs, which offers a more semantically grounded approach to assess cross-lingual alignment. We evaluate NeuronXA on several prominent multilingual LLMs (LLaMA, Qwen, Mistral, GLM, and OLMo) across two transfer tasks and three multilingual benchmarks. The results demonstrate that with only 100 parallel sentence pairs, NeuronXA achieves a Pearson correlation of 0.9556 with downstream tasks performance and 0.8514 with transferability. These findings demonstrate NeuronXA's effectiveness in assessing both cross-lingual alignment and transferability, even with a small dataset. This highlights its potential to advance cross-lingual alignment research and to improve the semantic understanding of multilingual LLMs.

papers.title: A circuit for predicting hierarchical structure in-context in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether induction heads in LLMs can support in-context learning of complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical dependencies, and how these induction heads themselves learn in-context.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs use adaptive induction heads that learn to attend to correct successor tokens in hierarchical contexts, supported by context matching heads that encode latent contexts, providing a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that LLMs use adaptive induction heads and context matching heads to learn hierarchical dependencies in-context, offering a mechanistic account of in-context learning for repetitive patterns.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads in LLMs can learn to attend to correct successor tokens in-context for sequences with hierarchical dependencies.
Adaptive induction heads are located in later layers, while static induction heads are in earlier layers.
Ablating induction heads severely reduces prediction accuracy, showing their causal role in in-context learning.
Context matching heads encode latent chunk identities and are causally involved in enabling induction heads to learn.
The proposed circuit of context matching heads feeding into induction heads explains hierarchical in-context learning, including in natural language ambiguous cases.
papers.limitation:
The study has not explored other types of in-context learning, such as abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
All learning analyzed happens non-verbally, without explicit verbal reasoning or deliberation.
future_direction: Study induction head behavior in abstract reasoning tasks like the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC).
Study induction head behavior in settings with verbal reasoning and deliberation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at in-context learning, the ability to use information provided as context to improve prediction of future tokens. Induction heads have been argued to play a crucial role for in-context learning in Transformer Language Models. These attention heads make a token attend to successors of past occurrences of the same token in the input. This basic mechanism supports LLMs' ability to copy and predict repeating patterns. However, it is unclear if this same mechanism can support in-context learning of more complex repetitive patterns with hierarchical structure. Natural language is teeming with such cases: The article "the" in English usually prefaces multiple nouns in a text. When predicting which token succeeds a particular instance of "the", we need to integrate further contextual cues from the text to predict the correct noun. If induction heads naively attend to all past instances of successor tokens of "the" in a context-independent manner, they cannot support this level of contextual information integration. In this study, we design a synthetic in-context learning task, where tokens are repeated with hierarchical dependencies. Here, attending uniformly to all successor tokens is not sufficient to accurately predict future tokens. Evaluating a range of LLMs on these token sequences and natural language analogues, we find adaptive induction heads that support prediction by learning what to attend to in-context. Next, we investigate how induction heads themselves learn in-context. We find evidence that learning is supported by attention heads that uncover a set of latent contexts, determining the different token transition relationships. Overall, we not only show that LLMs have induction heads that learn, but offer a complete mechanistic account of how LLMs learn to predict higher-order repetitive patterns in-context.

papers.title: Discovering Language-neutral Sub-networks in Multilingual Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual pre-trained language models learn language-neutral representations, and what is the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that multilingual language models contain language-neutral sub-networks that are topologically similar across languages and can be effectively transferred for cross-lingual tasks, but this transferability decreases at higher sparsity levels.
papers.conclusion: The results suggest that multilingual language models include separate language-neutral and language-specific components, with the language-neutral components playing a more prominent role in cross-lingual transfer performance.
papers.key_findings:
Winning tickets (sub-networks) can be found for each language and task at multiple sparsity levels, though performance degrades at higher sparsity.
Sub-networks for different languages have high parameter overlap, especially for NER and XNLI tasks, indicating language-neutral components.
Cross-lingual transfer of winning tickets is effective for XNLI and NER, but less so for MLM, and transfer performance degrades at higher sparsity.
The language-neutral components are more prominent in the middle to upper layers of the model.
Combining multiple languages during pruning can yield sub-networks that transfer better to low-resource languages.
papers.limitation:
Parameter overlap may not be a fine-grained measure for identifying language-neutral components, as small differences in cross-lingual performance do not strongly correlate with overlap.
Only the lottery ticket hypothesis is used for discovering sub-networks, while other pruning and masking methods may provide complementary or competing insights.
Due to computational limitations, the analysis is limited to three tasks and eleven languages, and new insights may emerge from a larger cross-section.
papers.abstract: Multilingual pre-trained language models transfer remarkably well on cross-lingual downstream tasks. However, the extent to which they learn language-neutral representations (i.e., shared representations that encode similar phenomena across languages), and the effect of such representations on cross-lingual transfer performance, remain open questions. In this work, we conceptualize language neutrality of multilingual models as a function of the overlap between language-encoding subnetworks of these models. We employ the lottery ticket hypothesis to discover sub-networks that are individually optimized for various languages and tasks. Our evaluation across three distinct tasks and eleven typologically-diverse languages demonstrates that sub-networks for different languages are topologically similar (i.e., language-neutral), making them effective initializations for cross-lingual transfer with limited performance degradation. 1

papers.title: The Semantic Hub Hypothesis: Language Models Share Semantic Representations Across Languages and Modalities
papers.research_question: To what extent do language models learn and use a shared semantic representation space across different languages and modalities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the semantic hub hypothesis, which posits that language models learn a shared representation space across languages and modalities, and provides evidence through representation similarity and intervention experiments.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that language models learn a shared semantic representation space (the semantic hub) that is anchored by the dominant language and is causally involved in processing across languages and modalities.
papers.key_findings:
Model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in intermediate layers.
The shared representation space is scaffolded by the model's dominant language (e.g., English) and can be interpreted via the logit lens.
This phenomenon extends to other data types: arithmetic expressions, code, images, and audio.
Interventions in the shared space using the dominant language affect model outputs in other data types, indicating causal usage.
The shared space is not just a byproduct but actively used during processing.
papers.limitation:
Chameleon-7B cannot answer more sophisticated reasoning questions about images, such as asking for a country flag or spatial relationships, even without interventions.
The logit lens analysis for audio is a lower bound because many words in labels (e.g., prepositions) are unlikely to be represented in the audio hidden states.
future_direction: Future work aimed at better controlling models using insights from the semantic hub hypothesis.
papers.abstract: Modern language models can process inputs across diverse languages and modalities. We hypothesize that models acquire this capability through learning a shared representation space across heterogeneous data types (e.g., different languages and modalities), which places semantically similar inputs near one another, even if they are from different modalities/languages. We term this the semantic hub hypothesis, following the hub-and-spoke model from neuroscience (Patterson et al., 2007) which posits that semantic knowledge in the human brain is organized through a transmodal semantic "hub" which integrates information from various modality-specific "spokes" regions. We first show that model representations for semantically equivalent inputs in different languages are similar in the intermediate layers, and that this space can be interpreted using the model's dominant pretraining language via the logit lens. This tendency extends to other data types, including arithmetic expressions, code, and visual/audio inputs. Interventions in the shared representation space in one data type also predictably affect model outputs in other data types, suggesting that this shared representations space is not simply a vestigial byproduct of large-scale training on broad data, but something that is actively utilized by the model during input processing.

papers.title: Emergence and Localisation of Semantic Role Circuits in LLMs
papers.research_question: Whether and how LLMs develop causally functional representations of semantic roles, specifically focusing on the localization, emergence dynamics, and cross-scale/cross-family generalization of semantic-role circuits.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces COMPASS, a causal-temporal method for discovering and tracking semantic-role circuits in LLMs, and finds that these circuits are highly localized, emerge via gradual refinement, and show partial transfer across scales and architectures.
papers.conclusion: LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure that exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures, suggesting that transformers encode predicate-argument binding via compact circuits.
papers.key_findings:
Semantic-role information is encoded in compact, role-specific circuits (89–92% attribution within ≤20 nodes).
These circuits emerge via continuous refinement rather than discrete phase transitions.
There is a structure-function dissociation: circuits stabilize structurally before becoming functionally indispensable.
Cross-scale and cross-family analysis shows moderate component reuse (24–51% node overlap) but divergent wiring.
Larger models reuse similar components while rewiring connections.
papers.abstract: Despite displaying semantic competence, large language models' internal mechanisms that ground abstract semantic structure remain insufficiently characterised. We propose a method integrating role-cross minimal pairs, temporal emergence analysis, and cross-model comparison to study how LLMs implement semantic roles. Our analysis uncovers: (i) highly concentrated circuits (89-94% attribution within 28 nodes); (ii) gradual structural refinement rather than phase transitions, with larger models sometimes bypassing localised circuits; and (iii) moderate cross-scale conservation (24-59% component overlap) alongside high spectral similarity. These findings suggest that LLMs form compact, causally isolated mechanisms for abstract semantic structure, and these mechanisms exhibit partial transfer across scales and architectures.

papers.title: Interpreting Context Look-ups in Transformers: Investigating Attention-MLP Interactions
papers.research_question: How do attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly, providing a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction.
papers.conclusion: Attention heads process context and use next-token neurons to help predict a word associated with, but not previously seen in that context, providing insight into how attention heads can work with MLP neurons to predict new words.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads can recognize contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron.
An automated method can explain and characterize interactions between attention heads and token-predicting neurons.
The head explanation score can be used to evaluate the quality of explanations.
The phenomenon is observed across different model families and sizes (GPT-2 and Pythia variants).
Ablation experiments confirm that the identified attention heads are causally involved in predicting the token.
papers.limitation:
Focus on max-activating behavior of neurons, which might overlook subtler activation patterns.
Reliance on a maximum of 30 prompts per neuron.
GPT-4 struggles with longer prompts and may generate poor explanations for certain patterns (like induction-style prompts).
Scope limited to neurons whose associated tokens are whole words and prompts shorter than 100 tokens.
future_direction: Investigate whether this phenomenon happens to such neurons throughout their range of activations.
Look into whether multiple attention heads could work with a single next-token neuron.
Look into whether a single attention head could work with multiple next-token neurons.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) is crucial for advancing their theoretical foundations and real-world applications. While the attention mechanism and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) have been studied independently, their interactions remain largely unexplored. This study investigates how attention heads and next-token neurons interact in LLMs to predict new words. We propose a methodology to identify next-token neurons, find prompts that highly activate them, and determine the upstream attention heads responsible. We then generate and evaluate explanations for the activity of these attention heads in an automated manner. Our findings reveal that some attention heads recognize specific contexts relevant to predicting a token and activate a downstream token-predicting neuron accordingly. This mechanism provides a deeper understanding of how attention heads work with MLP neurons to perform next-token prediction. Our approach offers a foundation for further research into the intricate workings of LLMs and their impact on text generation and understanding.

papers.title: Decomposing Natural Logic Inferences in Neural NLI
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether neural natural language inference (NLI) models capture the semantic features central to natural logic, specifically monotonicity and concept inclusion, in their internal representations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that monotonicity information is notably weak in the representations of popular NLI models that achieve high benchmark scores, and shows that fine-tuning on the HELP dataset improves both monotonicity feature encoding and performance on natural logic challenge sets.
papers.conclusion: The NLI-XY dataset provides evidence that explicit context monotonicity feature clustering in neural model representations corresponds to better performance on natural logic challenge sets, particularly for downward-monotone reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Models fine-tuned only on MNLI have poor performance on context monotonicity classification, indicating weak encoding of this feature.
Fine-tuning on the HELP dataset strengthens monotonicity features in model representations and improves performance on downward-monotone reasoning challenge sets.
Error analysis reveals that models often treat downward-monotone contexts as if they were upward-monotone, failing to discriminate between them systematically.
Probing shows that concept inclusion relations are generally better captured than context monotonicity in standard NLI models.
Visualization of representations indicates clearer clustering of monotonicity features after HELP fine-tuning, correlating with improved challenge set performance.
papers.limitation: The premise/hypothesis pairs in the NLI-XY dataset include generated examples that may not be consistently meaningful, raising questions about whether systematic behaviors should be observed on out-of-distribution examples.
future_direction: Further investigation of systematic behaviours on out-of-distribution examples generated from the permutation strategy in the NLI-XY dataset.
papers.abstract: In the interest of interpreting neural NLI models and their reasoning strategies, we carry out a systematic probing study which investigates whether these models capture the crucial semantic features central to natural logic: monotonicity and concept inclusion. Correctly identifying valid inferences in downward-monotone contexts is a known stumbling block for NLI performance, subsuming linguistic phenomena such as negation scope and generalized quantifiers. To understand this difficulty, we emphasize monotonicity as a property of a context and examine the extent to which models capture monotonicity information in the contextual embeddings which are intermediate to their decision making process. Drawing on the recent advancement of the probing paradigm, we compare the presence of monotonicity features across various models. We find that monotonicity information is notably weak in the representations of popular NLI models which achieve high scores on benchmarks, and observe that previous improvements to these models based on fine-tuning strategies have introduced stronger monotonicity features together with their improved performance on challenge sets.

papers.title: Journey to the Center of the Knowledge Neurons: Discoveries of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons and Degenerate Knowledge Neurons
papers.research_question: How is factual knowledge stored in multilingual pre-trained language models? Specifically, are there language-independent knowledge neurons and degenerate knowledge neurons?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients (AMIG) method for precise knowledge neuron localization and discovers two novel types of neurons: language-independent knowledge neurons, which store knowledge across languages, and degenerate knowledge neurons, which provide functional overlap for robust fact storage and can be used for fact-checking.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that their AMIG method enables precise knowledge localization and reveals two types of neurons that provide insights into knowledge storage, with language-independent neurons enabling cross-lingual editing and degenerate neurons enabling fact-checking.
papers.key_findings:
AMIG localizes knowledge neurons more precisely than previous methods, especially for Chinese datasets.
Knowledge neurons in m-BERT are primarily in the final layers, while in m-GPT they are distributed across early, middle, and final layers.
Language-independent knowledge neurons are concentrated in the final one or two layers and facilitate cross-lingual knowledge editing.
Degenerate knowledge neurons exist and can help PLMs detect wrong facts, improving fact-checking performance.
The existence of degenerate knowledge neurons is not dependent on multilingualism, as they are also found in monolingual models like BERT and GPT-2.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models (PLMs) contain vast amounts of factual knowledge, but how the knowledge is stored in the parameters remains unclear. This paper delves into the complex task of understanding how factual knowledge is stored in multilingual PLMs, and introduces the Architecture-adapted Multilingual Integrated Gradients method, which successfully localizes knowledge neurons more precisely compared to current methods, and is more universal across various architectures and languages. Moreover, we conduct an in-depth exploration of knowledge neurons, leading to the following two important discoveries: (1) The discovery of Language-Independent Knowledge Neurons, which store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language. We design cross-lingual knowledge editing experiments, demonstrating that the PLMs can accomplish this task based on language-independent neurons; (2) The discovery of Degenerate Knowledge Neurons, a novel type of neuron showing that different knowledge neurons can store the same fact. Its property of functional overlap endows the PLMs with a robust mastery of factual knowledge. We design fact-checking experiments, proving that the degenerate knowledge neurons can help the PLMs to detect wrong facts. Experiments corroborate these findings, shedding light on the mechanisms of factual knowledge storage in multilingual PLMs, and contribute valuable insights to the field. The code is available at https://github.com/heng840/AMIG.

papers.title: How does Alignment Enhance LLMs' Multilingual Capabilities? A Language Neurons Perspective
papers.research_question: How does multilingual alignment enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities from the perspective of language neurons?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a ternary classification of language neurons (specific, related, general) with an identification algorithm, and uses it to analyze how multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' capabilities by promoting shared neurons.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a ternary neuron classification and shows that multilingual alignment enhances LLMs' multilingual capabilities by promoting shared language-related neurons, providing valuable insights into the mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Language-related neurons shared by multiple languages are crucial for multilingual performance, not just language-specific neurons.
Multilingual alignment increases the reliance on shared language-related neurons rather than language-specific neurons.
LLMs' internal multilingual inference process can be divided into four functional stages based on neuron distributions.
Alignment enhances the activation of appropriate neuron types across different stages of inference.
Spontaneous multilingual alignment is facilitated by increased sharing of language-related neurons across languages.
papers.limitation:
Limited experiments on only two models and two datasets due to resource constraints.
No finer-grained analysis of neurons within the same layer.
future_direction: Perform more comprehensive analysis on different models and datasets.
Conduct finer-grained analysis of neurons within layers.
papers.abstract: Multilingual Alignment is an effective and representative paradigm to enhance LLMs' multilingual capabilities, which transfers the capabilities from the high-resource languages to the low-resource languages. Meanwhile, some research on language-specific neurons provides a new perspective to analyze and understand LLMs' mechanisms. However, we find that there are many neurons that are shared by multiple but not all languages and cannot be correctly classified. In this work, we propose a ternary classification methodology that categorizes neurons into three types, including language-specific neurons, language-related neurons, and general neurons. And we propose a corresponding identification algorithm to distinguish these different types of neurons. Furthermore, based on the distributional characteristics of different types of neurons, we divide the LLMs' internal process for multilingual inference into four parts: (1) multilingual understanding, (2) shared semantic space reasoning, (3) multilingual output space transformation, and (4) vocabulary space outputting. Additionally, we systematically analyze the models before and after alignment with a focus on different types of neurons. We also analyze the phenomenon of ''Spontaneous Multilingual Alignment''. Overall, our work conducts a comprehensive investigation based on different types of neurons, providing empirical results and valuable insights to better understand multilingual alignment and multilingual capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Focusing on Language: Revealing and Exploiting Language Attention Heads in Multilingual Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of multi-head self-attention in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs? Specifically, are there language-specific and language-general attention heads, and how can they be used to control model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LAHIS, a method to identify language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs, and shows how modulating these heads can control cross-lingual attention and improve multilingual performance with minimal parameters.
papers.conclusion: The work enhances interpretability of multilingual behaviors in LLMs from the perspective of MHA and presents practical approaches to strengthen multilingual capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
LAHIS reveals the existence of language-specific and language-general attention heads in multilingual LLMs.
Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer, allowing steering of model attention to target languages.
Modulating language-specific heads mitigates off-target language generation by suppressing English-heads.
A lightweight adaptation using a trainable matrix on language-specific heads improves multilingual question answering accuracy with only 14-20 parameters.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support multilingual understanding and generation. Meanwhile, efforts to interpret their internal mechanisms have emerged, offering insights to enhance multilingual performance. While multi-head self-attention (MHA) has proven critical in many areas, its role in multilingual capabilities remains underexplored. In this work, we study the contribution of MHA in supporting multilingual processing in LLMs. We propose Language Attention Head Importance Scores (LAHIS), an effective and efficient method that identifies attention head importance for multilingual capabilities via a single forward and backward pass through the LLM. Applying LAHIS to Aya-23-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Mistral-7B-v0.1, we reveal the existence of both language-specific and language-general heads. Language-specific heads enable cross-lingual attention transfer to guide the model toward target language contexts and mitigate off-target language generation issue, contributing to addressing challenges in multilingual LLMs. We also introduce a lightweight adaptation that learns a soft head mask to modulate attention outputs over language heads, requiring only 20 tunable parameters to improve XQuAD accuracy. Overall, our work enhances both the interpretability and multilingual capabilities of LLMs from the perspective of MHA.

papers.title: How and where does CLIP process negation?
papers.research_question: Which components of vision-language models are responsible for the model's understanding of negation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper adapts interpretability methods (causal tracing) to multimodal models, provides insights into how CLIP processes negation, and highlights limitations in the V ALSE benchmark.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates how interpretability methods can be applied to multimodal models, revealing the layered and partially localized processing of negation in CLIP, while also identifying dataset biases that affect benchmark performance.
papers.key_findings:
Negation processing in CLIP's text encoder is localized in early (layers 1-3) and late (layers 8-12) layers, with distributed representation in middle layers.
Specific attention heads in layer 4 show negator-selective attention and appear to shift negation information from the negator position to later positions in the sequence.
Dataset features such as the relative size of the subject in the image and the length of the caption/foil sequences correlate with classification performance, questioning the validity of V ALSE as a pure linguistic benchmark.
The first subject token plays a unique role when negation is in the caption, potentially due to the asymmetric task of searching for the subject's absence in the image.
Negator-selective attention patterns are consistent across correctly and incorrectly classified instances, suggesting they are not the sole determinant of classification success.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to the text encoder of CLIP and analyses simple effects of individual layer/position pairs; interactions between components are not explored.
Causal tracing methods are applied to a model capability (negation understanding) that is only moderately reliable (68.6% accuracy) on a relatively small dataset (n=490), which may limit the validity of the insights.
The explanations for the role of the first subject token when negation is in the caption are speculative and require further experimentation.
future_direction: Extend the methodology to other tasks and potentially other models to contextualize the degree of localisation found.
Analyse the interaction of certain layers or positions (e.g., by simultaneously patching activations in multiple places) to better understand the inner processes.
Conduct a larger study on dataset features (e.g., image brightness, contrast) that correlate with benchmark performance and compare with other VL benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Various benchmarks have been proposed to test linguistic understanding in pre-trained vision \& language (VL) models. Here we build on the existence task from the VALSE benchmark (Parcalabescu et al, 2022) which we use to test models' understanding of negation, a particularly interesting issue for multimodal models. However, while such VL benchmarks are useful for measuring model performance, they do not reveal anything about the internal processes through which these models arrive at their outputs in such visio-linguistic tasks. We take inspiration from the growing literature on model interpretability to explain the behaviour of VL models on the understanding of negation. Specifically, we approach these questions through an in-depth analysis of the text encoder in CLIP (Radford et al, 2021), a highly influential VL model. We localise parts of the encoder that process negation and analyse the role of attention heads in this task. Our contributions are threefold. We demonstrate how methods from the language model interpretability literature (such as causal tracing) can be translated to multimodal models and tasks; we provide concrete insights into how CLIP processes negation on the VALSE existence task; and we highlight inherent limitations in the VALSE dataset as a benchmark for linguistic understanding.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: An Analysis of Encoder Representations in Transformer-Based Machine Translation
papers.research_question: What kind of linguistic information (syntactic and semantic) is learned by the encoder of Transformer-based machine translation models, and how does it vary across layers and models with different translation quality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper analyzes encoder representations in Transformer-based machine translation and finds that specific attention heads capture syntactic dependencies, with lower layers encoding more syntax and higher layers more semantics.
papers.conclusion: The experimental evaluation sheds light on interesting findings about dependency relations and syntactic and semantic behavior across layers in Transformer encoder representations.
papers.key_findings:
Each layer has at least one attention head that encodes a significant amount of syntactic dependencies.
Lower layers tend to encode more syntactic information, while upper layers move towards semantic tasks.
The information about the length of the input sentence starts to vanish after the third layer.
Attention can be used to transfer knowledge between high- and low-resource languages, improving translation quality.
future_direction: Extend the analysis with probing tasks to evaluate other linguistic properties.
Use a recent evaluation dataset for analysis.
Analyze the attention weights between the encoder and the decoder.
papers.abstract: The attention mechanism is a successful technique in modern NLP, especially in tasks like machine translation. The recently proposed network architecture of the Transformer is based entirely on attention mechanisms and achieves new state of the art results in neural machine translation, outperforming other sequence-to-sequence models. However, so far not much is known about the internal properties of the model and the representations it learns to achieve that performance. To study this question, we investigate the information that is learned by the attention mechanism in Transformer models with different translation quality. We assess the representations of the encoder by extracting dependency relations based on self-attention weights, we perform four probing tasks to study the amount of syntactic and semantic captured information and we also test attention in a transfer learning scenario. Our analysis sheds light on the relative strengths and weaknesses of the various encoder representations. We observe that specific attention heads mark syntactic dependency relations and we can also confirm that lower layers tend to learn more about syntax while higher layers tend to encode more semantics.

papers.title: Strong hallucinations from negation and how to fix them
papers.research_question: How do language models handle negation and why do they produce strong hallucinations? How can we fix these hallucinations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a hybrid method (Λ) that treats negation as an operation over latent representations, constraining the evolution of distributions to eliminate strong hallucinations and improve performance on tasks with negation without requiring negative data.
papers.conclusion: The hybrid approach Λ effectively reduces strong hallucinations from negation and improves model performance on logical tasks by constraining the LM's distribution to respect logical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
Language models inevitably produce strong hallucinations due to their distribution over strings not respecting logical properties, as proven theoretically.
The proposed method Λ improves performance on masked knowledge retrieval (MKR) and natural language inference (NLI) tasks with negation.
Λ achieves 0 exact matches on MKR and significant accuracy improvements on NLI (e.g., 13% on one NLI dataset, 91% on another).
Λ uses models fine-tuned only on positive data, avoiding the need for sparse negative data.
Fine-tuned Llama combined with Λ showed a 27% accuracy improvement over Llama alone on ¬SNLI.
papers.limitation:
Tasks with long string output are beyond the paper's scope due to complex evaluations required.
Prompting procedures for Llama were unstable, with slight variations producing quite different results.
papers.abstract: Despite great performance on many tasks, language models (LMs) still struggle with reasoning, sometimes providing responses that cannot possibly be true because they stem from logical incoherence. We call such responses \textit{strong hallucinations} and prove that they follow from an LM's computation of its internal representations for logical operators and outputs from those representations. Focusing on negation, we provide a novel solution in which negation is treated not as another element of a latent representation, but as \textit{an operation over an LM's latent representations that constrains how they may evolve}. We show that our approach improves model performance in cloze prompting and natural language inference tasks with negation without requiring training on sparse negative data.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: How do Large Language Models Handle Multilingualism?
papers.research_question: How do large language models handle multilingualism?
papers.core_contribution: The paper hypothesizes and verifies a three-stage multilingual workflow (MWork) in LLMs, introducing PLND to detect language-specific neurons and showing how fine-tuning these neurons enhances multilingual abilities.
papers.conclusion: The verified MWork explains how LLMs handle multilingual tasks and provides an effective method for language-specific enhancement through fine-tuning language-specific neurons.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs convert multilingual inputs to English in intermediate layers for task-solving and then revert to the original language for generation.
Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection (PLND) can identify language-specific neurons without any labeled data.
Deactivating language-specific neurons causes significant performance drops in multilingual tasks but minimal impact on English.
Fine-tuning language-specific neurons with small datasets (e.g., 400 documents) improves multilingual performance without compromising other languages.
The multilingual workflow involves understanding layers, task-solving layers for reasoning and knowledge extraction, and generation layers.
papers.limitation: Fine-tuning with too many documents can lead to overfitting and performance deterioration due to disruption of original knowledge distribution.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across diverse languages. This study explores how LLMs handle multilingualism. Based on observed language ratio shifts among layers and the relationships between network structures and certain capabilities, we hypothesize the LLM's multilingual workflow ($\texttt{MWork}$): LLMs initially understand the query, converting multilingual inputs into English for task-solving. In the intermediate layers, they employ English for thinking and incorporate multilingual knowledge with self-attention and feed-forward structures, respectively. In the final layers, LLMs generate responses aligned with the original language of the query. To verify $\texttt{MWork}$, we introduce Parallel Language-specific Neuron Detection ($\texttt{PLND}$) to identify activated neurons for inputs in different languages without any labeled data. Using $\texttt{PLND}$, we validate $\texttt{MWork}$ through extensive experiments involving the deactivation of language-specific neurons across various layers and structures. Moreover, $\texttt{MWork}$ allows fine-tuning of language-specific neurons with a small dataset, enhancing multilingual abilities in a specific language without compromising others. This approach results in an average improvement of $3.6\%$ for high-resource languages and $2.3\%$ for low-resource languages across all tasks with just $400$ documents.

papers.title: Do Multilingual LLMs Think In English?
papers.research_question: Do multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation space closest to English, regardless of input and output languages?
papers.core_contribution: Multilingual LLMs perform semantic reasoning in a representation space biased towards English, even for non-English inputs and outputs, as evidenced by logit lens analysis and more effective steering with English-derived vectors.
papers.conclusion: Semantic decisions in LLMs are predominantly made in a representation space close to English, while non-lexical words are processed in the prompt language, and this behavior varies across models.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs route lexical words through English representation space before translating to the target language, while non-lexical words are not necessarily routed through English.
Steering non-English prompts is more effective using English steering vectors than vectors derived from the target language.
Facts are encoded in similar layers across languages, but models have a propensity to answer in English.
The degree of English-routing varies with model multilingualism and size, with more multilingual models routing less through English.
The latent representation structure allows interpolation between facts expressed in different languages while maintaining correctness, indicating shared semantic representations with language-specific components.
papers.limitation:
Tokenization varies across languages, complicating cross-lingual comparisons.
Models may have language confidence and confusion, affecting analysis.
Interpretability methods like steering depend on prompt steerability and may push activations outside the expected distribution.
Alternative methods like sparse autoencoders were not explored due to computational constraints.
future_direction: Developing more robust evaluation procedures for interpretability methods.
Exploring alternative methods like sparse autoencoders for cross-lingual analysis.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have multilingual capabilities and can solve tasks across various languages. However, we show that current LLMs make key decisions in a representation space closest to English, regardless of their input and output languages. Exploring the internal representations with a logit lens for sentences in French, German, Dutch, and Mandarin, we show that the LLM first emits representations close to English for semantically-loaded words before translating them into the target language. We further show that activation steering in these LLMs is more effective when the steering vectors are computed in English rather than in the language of the inputs and outputs. This suggests that multilingual LLMs perform key reasoning steps in a representation that is heavily shaped by English in a way that is not transparent to system users.

papers.title: Visualizing and Understanding Neural Models in NLP
papers.research_question: How do neural models achieve compositionality, building sentence meaning from the meanings of words and phrases?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces visualization strategies, including representation plotting and first-derivative saliency, to understand how neural models compose meaning, revealing phenomena like negation asymmetry and the superior focus of LSTMs on key words.
papers.conclusion: The proposed visualization methods offer initial insights into how neural models achieve meaning composition in NLP tasks, explaining aspects of LSTM performance and revealing semantic properties like negation asymmetry.
papers.key_findings:
LSTMs and Bi-LSTMs show a sharper focus on important keywords (like 'hate') compared to standard RNNs, filtering out irrelevant information.
The models capture the linguistic property of negative asymmetry, where 'not bad' is clustered with negative words rather than positive ones.
In concessive sentences, the models operate competitively, with the stronger clause dominating the final sentiment representation.
First-derivative saliency can identify which input words contribute most to a classification decision, though it is an approximation and may not capture all non-linear interactions.
Sequence-to-sequence autoencoders implicitly learn alignments, linking words to be predicted back to corresponding regions in the input.
papers.limitation:
First-derivative saliency is a rough approximation and might not suffice to deal with highly non-linear cases, as it does not capture all the information needed for visualization.
The variance-based salience measure can only be used in scenarios where word embeddings are parameters to learn from scratch.
The attempts only touch superficial points in neural models.
future_direction: Using the results of visualization to perform error analysis.
Understanding the strengths and limitations of different neural models.
papers.abstract: While neural networks have been successfully applied to many NLP tasks the resulting vectorbased models are very difficult to interpret. For example it's not clear how they achieve compositionality, building sentence meaning from the meanings of words and phrases. In this paper we describe strategies for visualizing compositionality in neural models for NLP, inspired by similar work in computer vision. We first plot unit values to visualize compositionality of negation, intensification, and concessive clauses, allowing us to see wellknown markedness asymmetries in negation. We then introduce methods for visualizing a unit's salience, the amount that it contributes to the final composed meaning from first-order derivatives. Our general-purpose methods may have wide applications for understanding compositionality and other semantic properties of deep networks.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: MPN: Leveraging Multilingual Patch Neuron for Cross-lingual Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can we perform cross-lingual model editing to update knowledge in multilingual models so that edits in one language generalize to other languages?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a simple method for cross-lingual model editing by training multilingual patch neurons, which can be easily adapted to existing fine-tuning based editing methods to improve their cross-lingual generalization.
papers.conclusion: MPN is an effective method for cross-lingual model editing that enhances cross-lingual generalization while maintaining locality and reliability, requiring minimal changes to existing editing approaches.
papers.key_findings:
Existing fine-tuning based editing methods possess a certain degree of cross-lingual editing effect, derived from the inherent cross-lingual transfer ability of the multilingual model.
The proposed MPN method improves cross-lingual editing performance without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology.
MPN achieves an average improvement of about 9% in CLG on the XFEVER dataset and about 12% on the XNLI dataset compared to baselines.
MPN demonstrates strong cross-lingual generalization and good locality, outperforming monolingual editing baselines.
The method is versatile and can be extended to other fine-tuning based editing methods.
papers.limitation:
The cross-lingual editing method is only applied to classification tasks (XFEVER and XNLI) and not to more complex tasks like question-answering.
The XFEVER dataset is created using machine translation without manual verification, which may affect translation quality.
future_direction: Utilize the Bi-zsRE dataset to assess cross-lingual editing performance on question-answering tasks.
Consider using larger models like GPT-4 to potentially improve translation results for dataset creation.
papers.abstract: Large language models are known for encoding a vast amount of factual knowledge, but they often becomes outdated due to the ever-changing nature of external information.
