A promising solution to this challenge is the utilization of model editing methods to update the knowledge in an efficient manner. However, the majority of existing model editing techniques are limited to monolingual frameworks, thus failing to address the crucial issue of cross-lingual knowledge synchronization for multilingual models. To tackle this problem, we propose a simple yet effective method that trains multilingual patch neuron to store cross-lingual knowledge. It can be easily adapted to existing approaches to enhance their cross-lingual editing capabilities. To evaluate our method, we conduct experiments using both the XNLI dataset and a self-constructed XFEVER dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method achieves improved performance in cross-lingual editing tasks without requiring excessive modifications to the original methodology, thereby showcasing its user-friendly characteristics. Codes will be released soon.

papers.title: Finding Highly Interpretable Prompt-Specific Circuits in Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuits in language models are prompt-specific rather than task-level, and introduces ACC++, a method to identify and analyze these prompt-specific circuits, revealing that prompts form families with representative circuits.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that circuits should be analyzed at the prompt level, and ACC++ enables scalable interpretability by identifying prompt-specific circuit families.
papers.key_findings:
ACC++ provides cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals compared to ACC.
Circuits in language models are prompt-specific, with no single circuit per task.
Prompts form clusters into families with similar circuits, allowing for representative circuits.
Signal analysis reveals stable routes and functional redundancy across prompt families.
An automated pipeline can generate interpretable explanations for circuit signals.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal circuits that language models use to solve tasks remains a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Most prior work identifies circuits at the task level by averaging across many prompts, implicitly assuming a single stable mechanism per task. We show that this assumption can obscure a crucial source of structure: circuits are prompt-specific, even within a fixed task. Building on attention causal communication (ACC) (Franco & Crovella, 2025), we introduce ACC++, refinements that extract cleaner, lower-dimensional causal signals inside attention heads from a single forward pass. Like ACC, our approach does not require replacement models (e.g., SAEs) or activation patching; ACC++ further improves circuit precision by reducing attribution noise. Applying ACC++ to indirect object identification (IOI) in GPT-2, Pythia, and Gemma 2, we find there is no single circuit for IOI in any model: different prompt templates induce systematically different mechanisms. Despite this variation, prompts cluster into prompt families with similar circuits, and we propose a representative circuit for each family as a practical unit of analysis. Finally, we develop an automated interpretability pipeline that uses ACC++ signals to surface human-interpretable features and assemble mechanistic explanations for prompt families behavior. Together, our results recast circuits as a meaningful object of study by shifting the unit of analysis from tasks to prompts, enabling scalable circuit descriptions in the presence of prompt-specific mechanisms.

papers.title: Interrogating the Explanatory Power of Attention in Neural Machine\n Translation
papers.research_question: To what extent are attention weights a reliable source of information for explaining the decisions made by a neural machine translation model?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that attention weights in neural machine translation are not a reliable explanation for model decisions, as counterfactual attention weights can produce the same output tokens, suggesting multiple contradictory explanations can exist for a single prediction.
papers.conclusion: Using attention weights to justify a model's prediction is not a reliable approach because alternative, contradictory attention weights can yield the same output.
papers.key_findings:
68% of function words and 21% of content words can be generated using counterfactual attention weights, indicating attention is unreliable for explanation.
Function word generation relies more on target context, while content word generation relies more on source context.
The EOS token generation is particularly unreliable to explain via attention, likely depending on special hidden units tracking translation length.
The last encoder state is a poor representation of the source context in an attentional model.
A high percentage of tokens (86%) can be generated by using only the maximally attended source state and uniformly combining others, suggesting highly tuned attention weights may not be necessary.
future_direction: Study the correlation between attention weights and importance measured by gradient-based methods.
Extend findings to other categories such as parts of speech (POS) or out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words.
Address interpretability of the copy mechanism in NMT.
Prove the correlation between attention and model predictions in more sophisticated attention models such as Transformer.
papers.abstract:
Attention models have become a crucial component in neural machine
translation (NMT). They are often implicitly or explicitly used to justify the
model's decision in generating a specific token but it has not yet been
rigorously established to what extent attention is a reliable source of
information in NMT. To evaluate the explanatory power of attention for NMT, we
examine the possibility of yielding the same prediction but with counterfactual
attention models that modify crucial aspects of the trained attention model.
Using these counterfactual attention mechanisms we assess the extent to which
they still preserve the generation of function and content words in the
translation process. Compared to a state of the art attention model, our
counterfactual attention models produce 68% of function words and 21% of
content words in our German-English dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that
attention models by themselves cannot reliably explain the decisions made by a
NMT model.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Decomposing Natural Logic Inferences for Neural NLI
papers.research_question: Do neural NLI models capture the semantic features central to natural logic (monotonicity and concept inclusion) in their internal representations, and how does this relate to their performance on natural logic inferences?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the NLI-XY probing dataset and shows that popular NLI models lack explicit representation of context monotonicity, but fine-tuning on the HELP dataset improves both feature extractability and performance on natural logic challenge sets.
papers.conclusion: Explicit context monotonicity feature clustering in neural model representations corresponds to better performance on natural logic challenge sets, and many popular models trained on MNLI lack this behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Models trained only on MNLI have poor performance on context monotonicity classification in their representations.
There is a correspondence between poor modeling of monotonicity features and poor performance on natural logic challenge sets.
Fine-tuning on the HELP dataset improves both the extractability of monotonicity features from representations and performance on challenge sets.
Decomposed error analysis shows models often treat downward monotone contexts as if they were upward monotone, failing to discriminate between them.
Visualization shows models fine-tuned on HELP exhibit stronger clustering of representations by context monotonicity.
papers.limitation: The permutation strategy for generating premise/hypothesis pairs may generate examples that are not consistently meaningful, which could affect the probing results.
future_direction: Investigate systematic behaviors on out-of-distribution examples generated by the permutation strategy.
papers.abstract: In the interest of interpreting neural NLI models and their reasoning strategies, we carry out a systematic probing study which investigates whether these modelscapture the crucial semantic features central to natural logic: monotonicity and concept inclusion.Correctly identifying valid inferences in downward-monotone contexts is a known stumbling block for NLI performance,subsuming linguistic phenomena such as negation scope and generalized quantifiers.To understand this difficulty, we emphasize monotonicity as a property of a context and examine the extent to which models capture relevant monotonicity information in the vector representations which are intermediate to their decision making process.Drawing on the recent advancement of the probing paradigm,we compare the presence of monotonicity features across various models.We find that monotonicity information is notably weak in the representations of popularNLI models which achieve high scores on benchmarks, and observe that previous improvements to these models based on fine-tuning strategies have introduced stronger monotonicity features together with their improved performance on challenge sets.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Idiom: Tracing Non-Compositionality in Language Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms do transformers use to process and make sense of natural language, specifically focusing on the processing of non-compositional idiomatic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a modified path patching algorithm for circuit discovery and uses it to identify specialized 'Idiom Heads' and a mechanism called 'augmented reception' in transformer models processing idioms, revealing how they balance computational efficiency and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that transformers process idioms in early layers with a sequential structure, identify specialized Idiom Heads, and reveal augmented reception as a mechanism for efficient attention, providing insights into non-compositional language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Idioms acquire their non-compositional (figurative) meaning in early layers (0-5) of the network, with a two-phase structure: cross-token attention in layers 0-2 followed by semantic integration in layers 3-5.
Specific attention heads ('Idiom Heads') consistently activate across multiple idioms, suggesting functional specialization for non-compositional language processing.
Each idiom employs a distinct direction in Query-Key space rather than a universal 'idiom direction'.
Early processing of idiom tokens creates 'augmented reception,' enhancing the receptivity of later attention heads to idiom-specific tokens, which is a mechanism for efficient attention allocation.
Most idiomatic processing occurs on the final token of the expression, deferring computation until all necessary context is available.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English idioms in a single model architecture (Gemma 2–2B).
Threshold determination for circuit discovery introduces subjective elements.
future_direction: Broader study of more idioms in multiple languages and transformer models to confirm generality.
Investigate whether similar patterns occur for other non-compositional phenomena, like grammatical constructions.
Further examples and investigation into augmented reception to deepen understanding of transformer information processing.
papers.abstract: We investigate the processing of idiomatic expressions in transformer-based language models using a novel set of techniques for circuit discovery and analysis. First discovering circuits via a modified path patching algorithm, we find that idiom processing exhibits distinct computational patterns. We identify and investigate ``Idiom Heads,'' attention heads that frequently activate across different idioms, as well as enhanced attention between idiom tokens due to earlier processing, which we term ``augmented reception.'' We analyze these phenomena and the general features of the discovered circuits as mechanisms by which transformers balance computational efficiency and robustness. Finally, these findings provide insights into how transformers handle non-compositional language and suggest pathways for understanding the processing of more complex grammatical constructions.

papers.title: One Mind, Many Tongues: A Deep Dive into Language-Agnostic Knowledge Neurons in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons in large language models, considering uncertainty across queries and languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces MATRICE, a method for localizing language-agnostic knowledge neurons by quantifying uncertainty across queries and languages, and constructs the RML-LAMA benchmark. It demonstrates these neurons' roles in cross-lingual editing, knowledge enhancement, and injection.
papers.conclusion: The proposed MATRICE method accurately localizes language-agnostic knowledge neurons, and these neurons are shown to be conducive to cross-lingual knowledge editing, enhancement, and injection.
papers.key_findings:
A significant proportion of language-agnostic knowledge neurons are distributed in the last few layers of LLMs.
Manipulating (suppressing/enhancing) language-agnostic knowledge neurons significantly affects knowledge expression across languages.
A single edit on language-agnostic knowledge neurons can simultaneously modify corresponding knowledge in all languages (cross-lingual editing).
Amplifying the activation of language-agnostic knowledge neurons improves prediction performance in low-resource languages.
Fine-tuning only parameters associated with language-agnostic knowledge neurons helps LLMs learn new knowledge while alleviating forgetting of old knowledge.
papers.limitation: The approach is based on knowledge neuron theory and focuses on factual knowledge, not yet extended to other types like commonsense or event knowledge.
future_direction: Extend the approach to investigate other types of knowledge, such as commonsense knowledge and event knowledge.
Adapt the method to new theoretical frameworks as the theory of knowledge neurons evolves.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have learned vast amounts of factual knowledge through self-supervised pre-training on large-scale corpora. Meanwhile, LLMs have also demonstrated excellent multilingual capabilities, which can express the learned knowledge in multiple languages. However, the knowledge storage mechanism in LLMs still remains mysterious. Some researchers attempt to demystify the factual knowledge in LLMs from the perspective of knowledge neurons, and subsequently discover language-agnostic knowledge neurons that store factual knowledge in a form that transcends language barriers. However, the preliminary finding suffers from two limitations: 1) High Uncertainty in Localization Results. Existing study only uses a prompt-based probe to localize knowledge neurons for each fact, while LLMs cannot provide consistent answers for semantically equivalent queries. Thus, it leads to inaccurate localization results with high uncertainty. 2) Lack of Analysis in More Languages. The study only analyzes language-agnostic knowledge neurons on English and Chinese data, without exploring more language families and languages. Naturally, it limits the generalizability of the findings. To address aforementioned problems, we first construct a new benchmark called Rephrased Multilingual LAMA (RML-LAMA), which contains high-quality cloze-style multilingual parallel queries for each fact. Then, we propose a novel method named Multilingual Integrated Gradients with Uncertainty Estimation (MATRICE), which quantifies the uncertainty across queries and languages during knowledge localization. Extensive experiments show that our method can accurately localize language-agnostic knowledge neurons. We also further investigate the role of language-agnostic knowledge neurons in cross-lingual knowledge editing, knowledge enhancement and new knowledge injection.

papers.title: Identifying and Evaluating Inactive Heads in Pretrained LLMs
papers.research_question: How prevalent are inactive attention heads in pretrained LLMs? The paper evaluates score functions that measure different ways a head can be inactive.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 12 score functions to identify inactive attention heads and shows that more than 12% of heads are inactive on average, and can be ablated while maintaining MMLU accuracy within 1%. It finds that measuring average head output norm is more effective than relying on attention sink patterns.
papers.conclusion: Understanding inactive attention heads requires looking beyond attention weights. The paper shows that more than 12% of heads can be zeroed out while maintaining accuracy within 1% of baseline, and average head output norm is the best signal for identifying inactive heads across model families.
papers.key_findings:
More than 12% of attention heads are inactive on average in pretrained LLMs.
Average Head Output Norm (LN) is the best score function for identifying inactive heads across model families.
Relying on attention sink patterns (Avg Weight of First Token) underestimates inactive heads by missing more than 7% on average.
Finetuning causes minimal changes in attention behavior.
Model scale has little effect on attention behavior until very large sizes.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on single forward passes as used in log-likelihood evaluations of multiple-choice benchmarks; analyzing generation is more complex and left for future work.
The best score function (AHON (LN)) requires computing the head output itself, which prevents compute savings when skipping heads.
future_direction: Analyzing generation tasks where zeroing out heads might have cascading effects.
Developing new architectures that leverage inactive heads for efficiency, such as dynamic pruning or KV cache compression.
Discovering better score functions that allow for compute savings by not requiring head output computation.
papers.abstract: Attention is foundational to large language models (LLMs), enabling different heads to have diverse focus on relevant input tokens. However, learned behaviors like attention sinks, where the first token receives the most attention despite limited semantic importance, suggest some heads may be inactive, and point to a significant source of computational redundancy. To analyze this phenomenon, we propose a taxonomy of 13 score functions that measure different ways a head can be inactive. Thresholding these scores allows us to analyze different sets of potentially inactive attention heads. We evaluate whether identified heads are inactive through model interventions, finding that more than 12% of attention heads are inactive on average, and can be ablated in specific contexts while maintaining MMLU accuracy to within 1% of the pretrained LLM. Across 3 model families, our score functions that measure the average norm of a head's output consistently identify inactive heads that would not have been found by score functions that rely solely on attention weights. We establish that relying on a score function that measures a first token attention sink would underestimate the prevalence of inactive heads, failing to identify more than 7% of inactive heads on average. We also show how measuring score distributions can provide insights into attention behavior. For instance, we find evidence that finetuning causes little to no change in attention behavior, and that even within the same model family, large model scales present markedly different attention behaviors.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Start Making Sense(s): A Developmental Probe of Attention Specialization Using Lexical Ambiguity
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in Transformer language models develop specialized attention patterns for word sense disambiguation, and how robust are these heads to stimulus perturbations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a developmental pipeline to probe attention specialization in Transformer LMs, using lexical ambiguity to identify and causally validate attention heads involved in word sense disambiguation, finding that larger models have more robust disambiguation heads.
papers.conclusion: Disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which are highly sensitive to cue position and part-of-speech (especially in smaller models), while larger models contain more robust disambiguation heads, highlighting the value of a developmental perspective in probing LM mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Disambiguation performance improves with model size but with diminishing returns, with 410M achieving 92% of the performance of 12B despite having 3% as many parameters.
Inflection points in disambiguation performance occur early in pre-training (e.g., at steps 1000 and 2000).
In Pythia-14M, specific attention heads (e.g., (3,1) and (3,2)) show attention patterns that covary with disambiguation performance.
In Pythia-410M, multiple heads across layers show robust disambiguation behavior, generalizing across stimulus perturbations like positional and part-of-speech changes.
Ablating identified heads causally impairs disambiguation performance, especially in Pythia-14M, confirming their functional role.
papers.abstract: Despite an in-principle understanding of self-attention matrix operations in Transformer language models (LMs), it remains unclear precisely how these operations map onto interpretable computations or functions--and how or when individual attention heads develop specialized attention patterns. Here, we present a pipeline to systematically probe attention mechanisms, and we illustrate its value by leveraging lexical ambiguity--where a single word has multiple meanings--to isolate attention mechanisms that contribute to word sense disambiguation. We take a "developmental" approach: first, using publicly available Pythia LM checkpoints, we identify inflection points in disambiguation performance for each LM in the suite; in 14M and 410M, we identify heads whose attention to disambiguating words covaries with overall disambiguation performance across development. We then stress-test the robustness of these heads to stimulus perturbations: in 14M, we find limited robustness, but in 410M, we identify multiple heads with surprisingly generalizable behavior. Then, in a causal analysis, we find that ablating the target heads demonstrably impairs disambiguation performance, particularly in 14M. We additionally reproduce developmental analyses of 14M across all of its random seeds. Together, these results suggest: that disambiguation benefits from a constellation of mechanisms, some of which (especially in 14M) are highly sensitive to the position and part-of-speech of the disambiguating cue; and that larger models (410M) may contain heads with more robust disambiguation behavior. They also join a growing body of work that highlights the value of adopting a developmental perspective when probing LM mechanisms.

papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Cognitive Mirrors: Exploring the Diverse Functional Roles of Attention Heads in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do attention heads in large language models specialize for different cognitive functions during complex reasoning tasks, and what are their properties and roles?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel interpretability framework and the CogQA dataset to analyze attention heads in LLMs, revealing that cognitive heads are sparse, functionally specialized, and hierarchically organized, and are crucial for reasoning tasks.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggests implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads exhibit functional specialization for specific cognitive functions (cognitive heads) and are sparse (only a small subset of heads are important for each function).
Cognitive heads are universal across different LLM architectures and model sizes.
Cognitive heads show layered functional organization, with different functions localizing to different layers (e.g., retrieval in middle layers, math in higher layers).
Cognitive heads exhibit functional clustering and hierarchical structure, where lower-level functions (e.g., retrieval) support higher-level reasoning.
Removing cognitive heads degrades performance on corresponding functions, while enhancing them improves reasoning accuracy, demonstrating their causal importance.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art performance in a variety of tasks, but remain largely opaque in terms of their internal mechanisms. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial to improve their reasoning abilities. Drawing inspiration from the interplay between neural processes and human cognition, we propose a novel interpretability framework to systematically analyze the roles and behaviors of attention heads, which are key components of LLMs. We introduce CogQA, a dataset that decomposes complex questions into step-by-step subquestions with a chain-of-thought design, each associated with specific cognitive functions such as retrieval or logical reasoning. By applying a multi-class probing method, we identify the attention heads responsible for these functions. Our analysis across multiple LLM families reveals that attention heads exhibit functional specialization, characterized as cognitive heads. These cognitive heads exhibit several key properties: they are universally sparse, vary in number and distribution across different cognitive functions, and display interactive and hierarchical structures. We further show that cognitive heads play a vital role in reasoning tasks - removing them leads to performance degradation, while augmenting them enhances reasoning accuracy. These insights offer a deeper understanding of LLM reasoning and suggest important implications for model design, training, and fine-tuning strategies.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Tracing the Roots of Facts in Multilingual Language Models: Independent, Shared, and Transferred Knowledge
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how factual knowledge is acquired and represented in multilingual language models, examining performance differences across languages, shared vs. independent representations, and mechanisms of cross-lingual transfer.
papers.core_contribution: This paper identifies three patterns of fact representation in multilingual language models—language-independent, cross-lingual shared, and cross-lingual transferred—and reveals limited effectiveness of cross-lingual knowledge transfer.
papers.conclusion: The study highlights the challenges in achieving effective cross-lingual transfer of factual knowledge and underscores the need for better representation learning and probing datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Factual probing performance varies across languages with moderate correlation to training data volume.
ML-LMs exhibit both language-independent and cross-lingual fact representations based on neuron activity patterns.
Cross-lingual knowledge transfer is limited and often localized to geographically proximate languages.
Easy-to-predict facts include shared entity tokens and naming cues, reducing apparent cross-lingual transfer.
Active neurons for facts in low-resource languages are more distributed in shallow layers compared to high-resource languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to encoder-based models (mBERT and XLM-R), and findings may not generalize to decoder-based models like BLOOM.
future_direction: Enhance cross-lingual fact representation learning in ML-LMs.
Develop a more precise factual probing dataset.
papers.abstract: Acquiring factual knowledge for language models (LMs) in low-resource languages poses a serious challenge, thus resorting to cross-lingual transfer in multilingual LMs (ML-LMs). In this study, we ask how ML-LMs acquire and represent factual knowledge. Using the multilingual factual knowledge probing dataset, mLAMA, we first conducted a neuron investigation of ML-LMs (specifically, multilingual BERT). We then traced the roots of facts back to the knowledge source (Wikipedia) to identify the ways in which ML-LMs acquire specific facts. We finally identified three patterns of acquiring and representing facts in ML-LMs: language-independent, cross-lingual shared and transferred, and devised methods for differentiating them. Our findings highlight the challenge of maintaining consistent factual knowledge across languages, underscoring the need for better fact representation learning in ML-LMs.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: On the Multilingual Ability of Decoder-based Pre-trained Language Models: Finding and Controlling Language-Specific Neurons
papers.research_question: How do decoder-based pre-trained language models handle multilingualism? Specifically, do language-specific neurons exist and how can they be controlled?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates the existence of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs and shows that intervening on these neurons can control the language of generated text.
papers.conclusion: The study provides insights into the activity of language-specific neurons in decoder-based multilingual PLMs, showing their existence and controllability, which can facilitate deeper understanding and future research.
papers.key_findings:
Language-specific neurons are unique to each language with little overlap (<5%).
These neurons are mainly distributed in the first and last few layers of the model.
Intervening on a small set of language-specific neurons (top and bottom 1000) can drastically change the probability of generating text in the target language.
The distribution pattern of language-specific neurons is consistent across languages and model variants.
For conditional text generation (machine translation), intervention on language-specific neurons can improve translation accuracy and BLEU score for some models (like Llama2).
papers.limitation:
Only analyzes open models with publicly available parameters, not closed models like ChatGPT or GPT-4.
Focuses on only six languages; other languages need to be examined in future studies.
Does not analyze encoder-decoder-based PLMs (e.g., mT5) due to architectural differences.
future_direction: Proposing language-specific model-compression methods.
Proposing new fine-tuning methods for downstream tasks to facilitate generalization to languages not included in the training dataset (e.g., only fine-tuning the middle-layer parameters).
Analysis of encoder-decoder-based PLMs remains important for future work.
papers.abstract: Current decoder-based pre-trained language models (PLMs) successfully demonstrate multilingual capabilities. However, it is unclear how these models handle multilingualism. We analyze the neuron-level internal behavior of multilingual decoder-based PLMs, Specifically examining the existence of neurons that fire ``uniquely for each language'' within decoder-only multilingual PLMs. We analyze six languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Chinese, and Japanese, and show that language-specific neurons are unique, with a slight overlap (< 5%) between languages. These neurons are mainly distributed in the models' first and last few layers. This trend remains consistent across languages and models. Additionally, we tamper with less than 1% of the total neurons in each model during inference and demonstrate that tampering with a few language-specific neurons drastically changes the probability of target language occurrence in text generation.

papers.title: The Validation Gap: A Mechanistic Analysis of How Language Models Compute Arithmetic but Fail to Validate It
papers.research_question: Why do LLMs struggle to detect arithmetic errors in their own outputs, and what internal mechanisms are responsible for error detection?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs have a structural dissociation between arithmetic computation (in higher layers) and validation (in middle layers), relying on consistency heads for surface-level alignment checks, which explains their difficulty in error detection.
papers.conclusion: Mechanistic interpretability provides valuable insights into how LLMs detect or fail to detect arithmetic errors, and the validation gap arises from structural dissociation between computation and validation.
papers.key_findings:
Circuits for arithmetic error detection are structurally similar across different models.
Error detection is governed by consistency heads—attention heads in lower to middle layers that check surface-level alignment of numerical values.
Arithmetic computation occurs in higher layers, while validation takes place in middle layers, leading to a structural dissociation.
Patching a small subset of consistency heads can control the model's error detection behavior.
Adding latent activations from higher layers to the residual stream in lower layers significantly enhances error detection, closing the validation gap.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to smaller LLMs and basic math word problems.
Circuit discovery may not be complete, i.e., identified circuits might not include all components involved in the task behavior.
future_direction: Study error detection in larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: The ability of large language models (LLMs) to validate their output and identify potential errors is crucial for ensuring robustness and reliability. However, current research indicates that LLMs struggle with self-correction, encountering significant challenges in detecting errors. While studies have explored methods to enhance self-correction in LLMs, relatively little attention has been given to understanding the models' internal mechanisms underlying error detection. In this paper, we present a mechanistic analysis of error detection in LLMs, focusing on simple arithmetic problems. Through circuit analysis, we identify the computational subgraphs responsible for detecting arithmetic errors across four smaller-sized LLMs. Our findings reveal that all models heavily rely on $\textit{consistency heads}$--attention heads that assess surface-level alignment of numerical values in arithmetic solutions. Moreover, we observe that the models' internal arithmetic computation primarily occurs in higher layers, whereas validation takes place in middle layers, before the final arithmetic results are fully encoded. This structural dissociation between arithmetic computation and validation seems to explain why smaller-sized LLMs struggle to detect even simple arithmetic errors.

papers.title: Incremental Processing of Principle B: Mismatches Between Neural Models and Humans
papers.research_question: Do GPT-based autoregressive neural language models use Principle B to restrict their incremental coreference processing like humans? Specifically, does Principle B block the influence of ungrammatical structural positions on pronoun prediction and cataphoric processing?
papers.core_contribution: GPT-based language models do not categorically ignore structural positions blocked by Principle B during incremental coreference processing, unlike humans. This mismatch suggests that certain aspects of human parsing behavior are not directly evidenced in linguistic data and may relate to properties of the training data.
papers.conclusion: Autoregressive neural models do not uniformly process pronouns like humans; they fail to capture qualitative patterns of incremental coreference processing and underestimate processing costs. Models appear to learn only those aspects of Principle B that have predictable reflexes in training data.
papers.key_findings:
For object pronouns (him) in positions where Principle B blocks co-indexation, all models exhibited a negative Gender Mismatch Effect (GMME), meaning they expected the pronoun to mismatch in gender with the grammatically unavailable antecedent.
For possessive pronouns (his), all models showed positive GMMEs across all structural positions, expecting gender agreement with antecedents.
In cataphoric object pronoun processing, larger models (GPT-J and GPT-3) showed no significant GMME when Principle B blocked coreference, aligning with human behavior, while smaller models (GPT-2 XL and GPT-Neo) showed a positive GMME.
Neural models greatly underestimate the magnitude of processing costs observed in humans, even in cases of qualitative overlap.
Analysis of the training data (the Pile) reveals a surface distribution bias where pronouns are more likely to mismatch in gender with antecedents in positions blocked by Principle B, suggesting models may overfit this pattern.
papers.limitation:
Whether models truly 'interpret' the correct coreference relations is unclear; techniques are limited for assessing if models comprehend meaning in a human-like fashion.
The study relies on stereotypical associations between nouns and pronouns, which does not cleanly map onto the real world (e.g., singular they is not considered).
The investigation is limited to English, due to resource availability and the focus of existing psycholinguistic work, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Future work might consider analyses of the attention mechanisms to dig deeper into what information models are using.
papers.abstract: Despite neural language models qualitatively capturing many human linguistic behaviors, recent work has demonstrated that they underestimate the true processing costs of ungrammatical structures. We extend these more fine-grained comparisons between humans and models by investigating the interaction between Principle B and coreference processing. While humans use Principle B to block certain structural positions from affecting their incremental processing, we find that GPT-based language models are influenced by ungrammatical positions. We conclude by relating the mismatch between neural models and humans to properties of training data and suggest that certain aspects of human processing behavior do not directly follow from linguistic data.Paper at CoNLL 2022

papers.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
papers.research_question: How can we perform fine-grained circuit analysis through MLP sublayers in transformers, given the polysemanticity of neurons? The paper proposes transcoders as a solution to enable input-invariant circuit analysis.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces transcoders, a method for approximating MLP sublayers with sparse, interpretable features, enabling input-invariant circuit analysis through MLPs.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders are an effective tool for decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits, enabling scalable and interpretable circuit analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders are as interpretable as SAEs and perform similarly or better in terms of sparsity and faithfulness.
Transcoders enable circuit analysis that factorizes into input-invariant and input-dependent terms, allowing for general claims about model behavior.
Blind case studies demonstrate that transcoders can reverse-engineer features without looking at activating examples.
Analysis of the GPT2-small greater-than circuit reveals new insights, such as the role of the MLP0 layer.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders may not capture all nuances of the original MLP, as seen in the 'caught' feature example where the transcoder did not accurately model the difference between 'was caught' and 'caught the ball'.
Blind case studies had some failures, indicating that circuit analysis with transcoders is not always perfect.
future_direction: Scaling transcoders to larger models.
Applying transcoders to more tasks and models.
papers.abstract: A key goal in mechanistic interpretability is circuit analysis: finding sparse subgraphs of models corresponding to specific behaviors or capabilities. However, MLP sublayers make fine-grained circuit analysis on transformer-based language models difficult. In particular, interpretable features -- such as those found by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) -- are typically linear combinations of extremely many neurons, each with its own nonlinearity to account for. Circuit analysis in this setting thus either yields intractably large circuits or fails to disentangle local and global behavior. To address this we explore transcoders, which seek to faithfully approximate a densely activating MLP layer with a wider, sparsely-activating MLP layer. We introduce a novel method for using transcoders to perform weights-based circuit analysis through MLP sublayers. The resulting circuits neatly factorize into input-dependent and input-invariant terms. We then successfully train transcoders on language models with 120M, 410M, and 1.4B parameters, and find them to perform at least on par with SAEs in terms of sparsity, faithfulness, and human-interpretability. Finally, we apply transcoders to reverse-engineer unknown circuits in the model, and we obtain novel insights regarding the "greater-than circuit" in GPT2-small. Our results suggest that transcoders can prove effective in decomposing model computations involving MLPs into interpretable circuits. Code is available at https://github.com/jacobdunefsky/transcoder_circuits/.

papers.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we discover and use sparse feature circuits, composed of interpretable features, to explain and edit model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits, which are causally implicated subnetworks of interpretable features, enabling detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, including a technique (SHIFT) for removing unintended signals without disambiguating data.
papers.conclusion: Sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding and editing of model behaviors, showing promise for interpretability and downstream applications.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse feature circuits are more interpretable and faithful than neuron circuits.
They can be used to understand model mechanisms, such as subject-verb agreement.
SHIFT can remove unintended signals from a classifier without access to disambiguating labeled data.
The method scales to automatically discover thousands of behaviors and their circuits in an unsupervised pipeline.
future_direction: Scaling to larger models
Improving the quality and coverage of SAEs
Applying feature circuits to a wider range of tasks and models
papers.abstract: We introduce methods for discovering and applying sparse feature circuits. These are causally implicated subnetworks of human-interpretable features for explaining language model behaviors. Circuits identified in prior work consist of polysemantic and difficult-to-interpret units like attention heads or neurons, rendering them unsuitable for many downstream applications. In contrast, sparse feature circuits enable detailed understanding of unanticipated mechanisms. Because they are based on fine-grained units, sparse feature circuits are useful for downstream tasks: We introduce SHIFT, where we improve the generalization of a classifier by ablating features that a human judges to be task-irrelevant. Finally, we demonstrate an entirely unsupervised and scalable interpretability pipeline by discovering thousands of sparse feature circuits for automatically discovered model behaviors.

papers.title: Dissecting Lottery Ticket Transformers: Structural and Behavioral Study of Sparse Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does iterative magnitude pruning affect the learned representations and internal structures of Transformers for neural machine translation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that iterative magnitude pruning degrades complex semantic knowledge first, causes higher layers to diverge and become less complex, shifts encoding burden to early layers, but leaves attention mechanisms largely unchanged.
papers.conclusion: The paper evaluates how unstructured pruning affects Transformer behavior while maintaining task performance, showing pruning degrades semantic knowledge before BLEU, early sparse layers better encode low-level information, representational changes occur in higher layers, and attention distributions remain similar.
papers.key_findings:
Complex semantic information is lost first during pruning, before BLEU decreases.
Model activations steadily diverge from unpruned representations, particularly at higher layers.
Information flow becomes more distributed in sparse Transformers: lower layers perform more encoding.
Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent across sparsities.
Encoder-decoder attention is the richest in representation, whereas decoder self-attention is the simplest.
papers.limitation:
BLEU is an imperfect measure of translation quality, so pruned models may perform worse than suggested.
The work focuses solely on magnitude pruning, which may not be representative of other pruning methods.
Probing classifiers measure correlation between model outputs and auxiliary information, not necessarily what information the model uses during its forward pass.
future_direction: Future work could analyze a model's encoded knowledge in other ways beyond probing.
Differences in how directly sparse and dense models encode information is an interesting question for future study, potentially using minimum description lengths.
papers.abstract: Recent work on the lottery ticket hypothesis has produced highly sparse Transformers for NMT while maintaining BLEU. However, it is unclear how such pruning techniques affect a model's learned representations. By probing Transformers with more and more lowmagnitude weights pruned away, we find that complex semantic information is first to be degraded. Analysis of internal activations reveals that higher layers diverge most over the course of pruning, gradually becoming less complex than their dense counterparts. Meanwhile, early layers of sparse models begin to perform more encoding. Attention mechanisms remain remarkably consistent as sparsity increases.

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
papers.research_question: What is the contribution of individual attention heads in multi-head attention models, and can a large percentage be pruned at test time without significantly impacting performance?
papers.core_contribution: Many attention heads in trained multi-head attention models are redundant and can be pruned without significant performance loss, with encoder-decoder attention being more reliant on multiple heads than self-attention.
papers.conclusion: Multi-head attention does not always fully leverage its theoretical expressiveness, and pruning heads can improve inference efficiency without harming performance, offering insights for more parameter-efficient models.
papers.key_findings:
Most attention heads can be individually removed at test time without a statistically significant drop in performance.
Some entire attention layers can be reduced to a single head without impacting performance.
A greedy pruning algorithm based on a gradient-derived importance score can remove 20-40% of heads without noticeable performance degradation.
Encoder-decoder attention layers are much more sensitive to pruning than self-attention layers.
The distinction between important and unimportant heads increases as training progresses, suggesting training dynamics play a role.
future_direction: A more principled investigation of the training dynamics of head importance.
Inspiring models that invest their parameters and attention more efficiently.
papers.abstract: Attention is a powerful and ubiquitous mechanism for allowing neural models to focus on particular salient pieces of information by taking their weighted average when making predictions. In particular, multi-headed attention is a driving force behind many recent state-of-the-art NLP models such as Transformer-based MT models and BERT. These models apply multiple attention mechanisms in parallel, with each attention "head" potentially focusing on different parts of the input, which makes it possible to express sophisticated functions beyond the simple weighted average. In this paper we make the surprising observation that even if models have been trained using multiple heads, in practice, a large percentage of attention heads can be removed at test time without significantly impacting performance. In fact, some layers can even be reduced to a single head. We further examine greedy algorithms for pruning down models, and the potential speed, memory efficiency, and accuracy improvements obtainable therefrom. Finally, we analyze the results with respect to which parts of the model are more reliant on having multiple heads, and provide precursory evidence that training dynamics play a role in the gains provided by multi-head attention.

papers.title: FuxiTranyu: A Multilingual Large Language Model Trained with Balanced Data
papers.research_question: How to build a multilingual large language model with balanced data to mitigate performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces FuxiTranyu, a multilingual LLM trained on balanced data, which shows competitive performance and more consistent multilingual representations compared to existing models.
papers.conclusion: FuxiTranyu is a strong open-source multilingual LLM, and balanced pre-training data is crucial for achieving consistent multilingual representations and performance.
papers.key_findings:
FuxiTranyu outperforms previous multilingual LLMs like BLOOM-7B1 and PolyLM-13B on several multilingual benchmarks.
Balanced pre-training data leads to more consistent multilingual representations across languages.
Neuron analysis reveals that deep layers are more language-specific and the importance of attention and MLP components varies across layers.
Languages with extremely limited resources (e.g., Bengali, Tamil) are allocated fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model achieves high performance on summarization tasks, outperforming baseline models on XL-Sum.
papers.limitation:
Languages with extremely limited resources, such as Bengali and Tamil, are allocated with fewer neurons and perform poorly.
The model underperforms in some tasks (e.g., m-ARC, m-MMLU) due to limited training data for English.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated prowess in a wide range of tasks. However, many LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between high- and low-resource languages. To mitigate this challenge, we present FuxiTranyu, an open-source multilingual LLM, which is designed to satisfy the need of the research community for balanced and high-performing multilingual capabilities. The base model, FuxiTranyu-8B, features 8 billion parameters and is trained from scratch on meticulously balanced multilingual data that contains 600 billion tokens covering 43 natural languages and 16 programming languages. We also develop two instruction-tuned models: FuxiTranyu-8B-SFT which is fine-tuned on a diverse multilingual instruction dataset, and FuxiTranyu-8B-DPO which is further refined with DPO on a preference dataset for enhanced alignment ability. Extensive experiments on a wide range of multilingual benchmarks demonstrate the competitive performance of FuxiTranyu against existing multilingual LLMs, e.g., BLOOM-7B, PolyLM-13B, and Mistral-7B-Instruct. Both neuron and representation interpretability analyses reveal that FuxiTranyu achieves consistent multilingual representations across languages. To promote further research into multilingual LLMs, we release both the base and instruction-tuned FuxiTranyu models together with 58 pre-training checkpoints at HuggingFace (see https://huggingface.co/TJUNLP/FuxiTranyu-8B) and Github (see https://github.com/tjunlp-lab/FuxiTranyu).

papers.title: Benchmarking and Understanding Compositional Relational Reasoning of LLMs
papers.research_question: What is the capability of existing transformer large language models (LLMs) in solving compositional relational reasoning (CRR) tasks, and what are the underlying mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) benchmark for evaluating compositional relational reasoning in LLMs, revealing their deficiency, and discovers core circuits and True/False attention heads that are fundamental for CRR.
papers.conclusion: The GAR benchmark is challenging for mainstream LLMs and reveals a fundamental deficiency in compositional relational reasoning. Mechanistic interpretability analysis discovers reusable core circuits and identifies True/False attention heads that play fundamental roles in CRR across models and tasks.
papers.key_findings:
GAR is challenging for existing LLMs, with performance dropping significantly for harder tasks and the compositionality gap increasing with model scale.
Attribution patching reveals core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different GAR tasks, including a truthfulness sub-circuit and an in-context learning sub-circuit.
Intervention experiments show that correct functioning of identified vital attention heads (e.g., predicting, pre-predicting, higher-order local, induction, and relating heads) significantly impacts task performance.
Two classes of higher-order relating heads (True and False heads) are identified whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks.
The activation patterns of the True/False heads generalize to other datasets (SNLI and GoT), indicating they encode information for truthfulness classification beyond GAR.
papers.limitation: The circuit discovery is done manually without using automatic circuit discovery methods, which is left for future work.
future_direction: Automatic circuit discovery methods for larger models and more complex circuits.
papers.abstract: Compositional relational reasoning (CRR) is a hallmark of human intelligence, but we lack a clear understanding of whether and how existing transformer large language models (LLMs) can solve CRR tasks. To enable systematic exploration of the CRR capability of LLMs, we first propose a new synthetic benchmark called Generalized Associative Recall (GAR) by integrating and generalizing the essence of several tasks in mechanistic interpretability (MI) study in a unified framework. Evaluation shows that GAR is challenging enough for existing LLMs, revealing their fundamental deficiency in CRR. Meanwhile, it is easy enough for systematic MI study. Then, to understand how LLMs solve GAR tasks, we use attribution patching to discover the core circuits reused by Vicuna-33B across different tasks, and a set of vital attention heads. Intervention experiments show that the correct functioning of these heads significantly impacts task performance. Especially, we identify two classes of heads whose activations represent the abstract notion of true and false in GAR tasks respectively. They play fundamental roles in CRR across various models and tasks.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Causal Head Gating: A Framework for Interpreting Roles of Attention Heads in Transformers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models in a causal manner?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for causal interpretation of attention heads, and shows that LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits, head roles are low modularity, and instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: CHG is a flexible and scalable method for identifying causally relevant attention heads, revealing the distributed and context-dependent nature of computation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
CHG scores yield causal insight validated via ablation and causal mediation analysis.
LLMs contain multiple sparse task-sufficient sub-circuits.
Individual head roles depend on interactions with others (low modularity).
Instruction following and in-context learning rely on separable mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
CHG does not reveal the precise computations performed by individual heads.
Occasional divergence between G+ and G- scores.
Head roles are context-dependent and vary across runs.
future_direction: Build on these tools to develop circuit-level explanations of how models implement complex behaviors.
papers.abstract: We present causal head gating (CHG), a scalable method for interpreting the functional roles of attention heads in transformer models. CHG learns soft gates over heads and assigns them a causal taxonomy - facilitating, interfering, or irrelevant - based on their impact on task performance.
